<p style="margin: 0 0 0.5rem 0;">At this sample size, ${Math.round(share * 1000) / 10}% of ${d}-decimal endings are attainable.</p>`
    : html`<p style="margin: 0.8rem 0 0.5rem 0;">Enter a mean and a whole-number sample size of up to ${cols} to select a cell.</p>`
  const legendSquare = (fill, stroke) => `<svg width="14" height="14" style="vertical-align: -2px;"><rect x="1" y="1" width="12" height="12" fill="${fill}" stroke="${stroke}"/></svg>`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = `<span>${legendSquare("black", "black")} Attainable</span>
    <span>${legendSquare("white", "rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.8)")} Impossible</span>
    <span>${legendSquare("none", blue)} Selected cell</span>`
  return html`${message}${plot}${legend}`
}







roundingOptions = new Map([["Up or down", "up_or_down"], ["Half up", "up"], ["Half down", "down"], ["Half to even", "even"], ["Truncation", "trunc"], ["Up or down, or truncation", "up_or_down_trunc"]])
roundingPhrases = ({up_or_down: "halves rounded up or down", up: "halves rounded up", down: "halves rounded down", even: "halves rounded to even", trunc: "values truncated", up_or_down_trunc: "halves rounded up or down, or values truncated"})
function grimEndings(nk, d, rounding) {
  // which of the 10^d endings at d decimals some mean of nk whole numbers is reported as. only the decimal part of a
  // mean matters, so the sums S = 0 to nk - 1 cover every case. the arithmetic is in whole numbers, so that exact
  // halves stay exact: the mean S / nk is S x 10^d / nk reporting steps
  const scale = 10 ** d, reached = new Uint8Array(scale)
  const rules = {up_or_down: ["up", "down"], up_or_down_trunc: ["up", "down", "trunc"]}[rounding] ?? [rounding]
  for (let S = 0; S < nk; S++) {
    const num = S * scale, q = (num - (num % nk)) / nk, twice = 2 * (num % nk)
    for (const rule of rules) {
      // twice the remainder is above, below, or equal to nk when the mean is above, below, or exactly at a half
      const v = rule === "trunc" ? q
        : twice > nk ? q + 1 : twice < nk ? q
        : rule === "up" ? q + 1 : rule === "down" ? q : q % 2 === 0 ? q : q + 1
      reached[v % scale] = 1
    }
  }
  return reached
}
























Figure 12.1: GRIM-consistent (black) and GRIM-inconsistent (white) endings of a mean, by sample size. Only the decimal part of a mean matters: if 2.49 is attainable for a given N, so are 0.49 and 8.49.



Brown and Heathers give the approximation: with two decimals and N below 100, a random value is consistent in about N% of cases. More generally the pass rate is close to N × items / 10d, up to a maximum of 1. It is not exactly that under the lenient rounding rule, because sample sizes that produce exact halves have higher pass rates (Section 12.2.2.1).

12.2.2.1 The cost of leniency
Every rounding practice that the test accommodates widens the band of exact values that count as a match, so more wrong values pass. The trade-off is unavoidable: a lenient test raises fewer false alarms and misses more errors.
To see its size, we work out the pass rate under different combinations of rounding rules. For each sample size, we take every mean that whole numbers can produce, round it under each rule with the {roundwork} package (which {scrutiny} uses for its own rounding), and count how many of the 100 possible two-decimal endings are reached. For the “up” and “up or down” rules, these counts are the same as the share of endings that {scrutiny}’s grim() accepts. We use the same function for the pass rates in the rest of the chapter.
Here we use the pass rate to compare three versions of the test.








Figure 12.2: Share of all two-decimal values that pass GRIM for a single item, by sample size, under three sets of accommodated rounding practices.





Under the strict rule the pass rate is exactly N/100. Allowing halves to go either way makes no difference at most sample sizes, because exact halves only arise when the sample size is a multiple of 8. Where they do arise the effect can be large: at N = 40 the pass rate is 60% instead of 40%, and at N = 80 every value passes, so the lenient test already stops being informative there. Allowing truncation as well costs more, and at almost every sample size: the pass rate climbs about one and a half times as fast, and from about N = 67 nothing can fail. The exceptions are sample sizes that divide evenly into 100, such as 20, 25, and 50, where means have no further decimals to cut off.
The same idea carries over to the other tests. For percentages, the pass rate is about N / 10d+2. For GRIMMER, Figure 12.4 in Section 12.3 shows the joint pass rate for a random mean and SD, which is far lower than for GRIM alone in small samples. {scrutiny} reports the fail rate under the strict rule as the probability column of grim_map(), and grim_probability() returns it directly.
Is a random number the right comparison? The pass rate assumes that a wrong value is equally likely to be any printable value. Real wrong values are not like that. A typo usually changes one digit. A value copied from the wrong row is another real mean. People who invent numbers favour some final digits and avoid others. The uniform assumption is best treated as a reference point, not a model of how errors arise, and conclusions that depend on it should be checked against other reference distributions. The grim_sensitivity() function in {strait} does this for digit preferences.



12.2.3 When GRIM is uninformative
The most important practical fact about GRIM is where its pass rate reaches 100%. From that point every printable value passes, the test cannot fail, and a pass tells us nothing. The test can only fail when the attainable means are further apart than the reporting steps, which requires
\[N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}\]
where d is the number of reported decimals. With the usual two decimals, GRIM applies to fewer than 100 participants on a single item. At or above that, every two-decimal value is attainable and every mean passes. Brown and Heathers call variables below this limit GRIM-testable. Allowing halves to be rounded either way can end the test slightly earlier, at sample sizes that produce exact halves. At N = 80, for example, every two-decimal value passes (Section 12.2.2.1). The GRIM plot in Section 12.3.1 reports the test as uninformative in both cases.
Use Figure 12.3 to see where the limit falls for different numbers of decimals, items averaged, and rounding rules.




viewof prDigits = Inputs.select([1, 2, 3], {label: "Decimal places", value: 2})
viewof prItems = Inputs.number({label: "Items averaged into each participant's score", value: 1, step: 1, min: 1, width: 90})
viewof prRounding = Inputs.select(roundingOptions, {label: "Rounding", value: "up_or_down"})























{
  const d = prDigits, scale = 10 ** d, k = prItems
  if (!Number.isInteger(k) || k < 1) return html`<p style="font-weight: 600;">Enter a whole number of items.</p>`
  const blue = "#2780e3"
  const maxN = Math.max(10, Math.ceil(1.15 * scale / k))
  const rows = d3.range(1, maxN + 1).map(n => ({n, pass: grimEndings(n * k, d, prRounding).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / scale, approximation: Math.min(1, n * k / scale)}))
  // the sample size from which the test can never fail, and any smaller ones where it happens not to be able to
  let from = maxN + 1
  while (from > 1 && rows[from - 2].pass === 1) from--
  const isolated = rows.filter(r => r.n < from && r.pass === 1).map(r => r.n)
  const margins = {marginLeft: 64, marginRight: 28, marginTop: 20, marginBottom: 45}
  const frame = Math.min(520, width - margins.marginLeft - margins.marginRight)
  const plotWidth = frame + margins.marginLeft + margins.marginRight
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: plotWidth, height: Math.round(frame * 0.6) + margins.marginTop + margins.marginBottom, ...margins,
    x: {label: "Sample size (N)", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 38, domain: [0, maxN]},
    y: {label: "Values that pass", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 54, domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
    style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "n", y: "approximation", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "n", y: "pass", stroke: blue, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      from <= maxN ? Plot.ruleX([from], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6}) : null,
      from <= maxN ? Plot.text([{}], {x: from, y: 1, text: () => `N = ${from}`, dy: -8, textAnchor: from > maxN * 0.8 ? "end" : "start", dx: from > maxN * 0.8 ? -4 : 4, fontWeight: 600}) : null,
      Plot.dot(isolated.map(n => ({n})), {x: "n", y: () => 1, r: 4, fill: blue})
    ]
  })
  const what = `With ${d} ${d === 1 ? "decimal" : "decimals"}, ${k} ${k === 1 ? "item" : "items"} averaged, and ${roundingPhrases[prRounding]}`
  const also = isolated.length ? `, and also at N = ${isolated.length > 6 ? isolated.slice(0, 6).join(", ") + ", …" : isolated.join(", ")}` : ""
  const message = from <= 1 ? `${what}, GRIM cannot fail at any sample size.` : `${what}, GRIM cannot fail from N = ${from} onwards${also}.`
  const legend = html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.25rem 1.25rem; justify-content: center; font-size: 0.85rem; margin-top: 0.25rem; max-width: ${plotWidth}px;">`
  legend.innerHTML = `<span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="${blue}" stroke-width="2"/></svg> Pass rate</span>
    <span><svg width="28" height="10"><line x1="0" x2="28" y1="5" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.5" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/></svg> Approximation, <i>N</i> × items / 10<sup><i>d</i></sup></span>`
  return html`<p style="font-weight: 600; margin: 0.8rem 0 0.5rem 0;">${message}</p>${plot}${legend}`
}








Figure 12.3: GRIM pass rates by sample size, for the chosen number of decimals, items averaged, and rounding rule. The dashed line is the approximation N × items / 10d. The vertical line marks the sample size from which GRIM can no longer fail.



Changing the number of decimals or the items averaged does not change the shape of the line, because only the product N × items matters. It only changes where the line reaches 100%: at N = 10 for a single item reported to one decimal, and at N = 1,000 for a single item reported to three. A five-item mean score at two decimals is exhausted by N = 20, and a ten-item mean score at one decimal cannot be tested at any sample size.
Two consequences follow.
Decimals matter as much as sample size. Each extra reported decimal multiplies the reach of the test by ten. A mean reported to three decimals is testable up to N = 999, and one reported to a single decimal only up to N = 9. Supplementary tables, which often report more decimals than the main text, are therefore worth checking.
Record every value exactly as printed. “3.50” has two decimals and “3.5” has one, and GRIM gives different answers for them. Spreadsheets and statistical software drop trailing zeros silently, so the number of decimals has to be recorded when the value is read from the article. It cannot be recovered afterwards from a stored number.






NoteThe maths of when GRIM cannot be used





In units of the sum, the interval \(Nk \times I(\tilde{M})\) has width
\[2\,\delta\,Nk = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}}.\]
An interval of width 1 or more that includes at least one of its ends always contains a whole number. So whenever \(Nk \ge 10^{d}\), every reported value is consistent and the test cannot fail. This is the condition \(N \times \text{items} < 10^{d}\) given above.
When \(Nk < 10^{d}\), neighbouring attainable means are more than one reporting step apart, so each rounds to a different reported value. The \(Nk\) attainable means in any unit interval, such as from 3.00 up to 4.00, therefore account for exactly \(Nk\) of the \(10^{d}\) values that can be printed there. Under a strict rounding rule, the share of printable values that are consistent is
\[p = \frac{Nk}{10^{d}},\]
and the share that are inconsistent is \(q = 1 - p\). These are the pass rate and fail rate described in Section 12.2.2. Under the lenient rule, an attainable mean that falls exactly halfway between two printable values makes both of them consistent, so \(p\) is larger by one printable value for each such tie.
A percentage reported to \(d\) decimals is a proportion reported to \(d + 2\) decimals, with \(k = 1\). Everything above applies with \(d + 2\) in place of \(d\).





12.2.4 Interpreting a consistent result
A failure and a pass are not mirror images. A failure shows that something among the reported mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding is not as stated (Section 12.5). A pass only shows that the mean was not caught, and what that is worth depends on how likely a wrong value would have been to be caught.
The pass rate answers this, because it describes the counterfactual of a value that has nothing to do with the data. Suppose a mean from 12 participants passes GRIM. A value picked at random would have passed only about 12% of the time, so the pass rules out most ways of being wrong. Now suppose a mean from 90 participants passes. A random value would have passed about 90% of the time, so the pass is almost exactly what we would expect whether the mean was correct or not. From 100 participants on, a pass carries no information at all.
A consistent result is therefore best reported as “not shown to be impossible”, together with its pass rate, and never as evidence that a value is correct. The same holds for a set of values: ten random values would all pass at N = 90 about a third of the time, but three would all pass at N = 12 less than once in 500 tries.

title: 12  Granularity methods ✎ Draft
text:
12.4 What large-scale applications have found

36 of 71
GRIM-testable psychology articles contained at least one mean that was inconsistent with its reported sample size (Brown & Heathers, 2017).

The only systematic application of GRIM to a sample of the literature that we know of is in the article that introduced it. Brown & Heathers (2017) searched the 2011–2015 issues of Psychological Science, the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, and the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology for articles containing the word “Likert”, and examined 260 of them. Of these, 189 (73%) had no GRIM-testable data, mostly because their samples were too large. In the remaining 71:

35 (49%) reported all testable means consistently.
15 (21%) had one or two inconsistencies that looked like typographical errors.
5 (7%) had a small number of inconsistencies that might affect the main results.
16 (23%) had a larger number of inconsistencies, often at several points in the article. In some of these, more than half of the testable values were inconsistent.

The authors requested the data for the 21 articles in the last two categories. They obtained data from eight authors, and a ninth provided enough information to check the means. Five authors refused, four promised data that did not arrive, and the rest could not be reached or did not reply. In all nine cases that could be checked, GRIM had identified at least one real problem, and three articles needed formal corrections.
The causes they found in these nine articles are instructive, because none of them is fraud and most are mundane: sample sizes that differed from those reported (in five of the nine cases), a spreadsheet formula that included the wrong cells, values copied incorrectly, the stepped rounding of SDs described in Note 12.1, and, in one case, an analysis error serious enough for the authors to issue a correction once they noticed it while preparing the data. In one case, Brown and Heathers had themselves made an error by overlooking that a measure was a multi-item composite.
The nine were the articles whose authors cooperated. The other twelve, whose authors refused the request for data, did not send it, or did not reply, were left unresolved in the published article. A later preprint by one of its authors reports what Brown and Heathers had concluded about them (Heathers, 2024). All twelve contained multiple inconsistencies, and three contained what the authors considered definite hallmarks of systematic data manipulation. These figures were removed from the 2017 article because they were judged “sufficiently speculative and controversial at the time of publication”. Taken together, they put the share of the 71 GRIM-testable articles with hallmarks of data manipulation at between 3 of 71 (4.2%) and 12 of 71 (16.9%). The range is wide for two reasons. A refusal to share data is not in itself evidence of manipulation, and the three clearest cases rest on the authors’ judgement of the reported values, without the data that would settle them.
Granularity tests also became known through case studies. GRIM and GRIMMER were among the tools used in the reanalysis of four articles from the Cornell Food and Brand Lab (Zee et al., 2017).

12.5 Assumptions and sources of false positives and false negatives
The previous sections introduced the assumptions of granularity tests one at a time. Table 12.3 collects them. A false positive is a correctly reported value that the test flags as impossible. A false negative is an incorrect value that the test passes.



Table 12.3: Assumptions of granularity tests and what happens when they fail.










Assumption
If it is wrong
Guard against it by




The N behind this statistic is the one we used
False positives. Cell sizes assumed equal when they are not, N before exclusions used in place of N analysed, item-level missing data
Looking for cell sizes in tables, degrees of freedom, and flow diagrams. Searching for an N that makes all values consistent


The number of items averaged into each participant’s score is right
False positives if a mean score is tested as a single item. False negatives if a sum score is tested as a mean score, or if the number of items in the scale is used for a sum score
Reading the measures section for how the scale was scored. Items averaged is 1 for single items, whole-number variables, and sum scores


The data are whole numbers
False positives
Checking the response format


The mean is a simple average of observed scores, not a model estimate
False positives. Estimated marginal means, least-squares means, covariate-adjusted means, and conditional means or predicted values from a regression or mixed model are not averages of whole numbers, even when the raw scores are
Reading table notes and the analysis section for words such as adjusted, estimated, marginal, model-based, or predicted. Testing only raw descriptive means


No missing values were imputed
False positives. Mean imputation, regression imputation, and multiple imputation produce values that are not whole numbers, and a mean pooled over several imputed datasets is an average of means. Methods that copy observed values, such as last observation carried forward, keep whole numbers but change which N applies
Reading the missing-data section. Comparing the N analysed with the number who completed the measure. Testing complete-case statistics where they are reported


The rounding practice is one we allowed for
False positives
Using the lenient rule, and considering truncation and stepped rounding before reporting a failure


The value was extracted correctly
False positives. Dropped trailing zeros, values read from the wrong column, PDF conversion faults, the assessor’s own typos
Re-reading every flagged value in the original article


The SD uses the sample formula, dividing by N − 1 (GRIMMER)
False positives. An SD calculated with the population formula, dividing by N (the default in NumPy, and Excel’s STDEV.P), is smaller by a factor of √((N − 1)/N), which is enough to change the second decimal
Re-testing with the reported SDs multiplied by √(N/(N − 1))






False negatives have a different set of causes, most of which cannot be fixed.

The test cannot fail. When N × items is 100 or more at two decimals, GRIM passes everything.
Chance. A wrong value can land on an attainable one. For a wrong value picked at random, the probability is the pass rate (Section 12.2.2).
Leniency. Every accommodated rounding practice lets more wrong values through.

The asymmetry between the two outcomes is the main thing to take from this section. A failure is strong evidence that something is misreported, provided the checks in Table 12.3 have been made, and no evidence about what or why. A pass is weak evidence of anything. Brown and Heathers make the same point: the number of GRIM failures in an article is a conservative estimate of the number of errors.

12.7 Other granularity methods: GRIM-U
Granularity is not restricted to means and SDs of integer data. Any statistic that is calculated from a finite number of discrete outcomes can take only a finite set of values, so many other granularity tests could in principle be developed. Means and SDs were simply the first applications.
GRIM-U (Heathers & Grimes, 2025) applied the principle to the Mann-Whitney U test. It relies on the granularity not of the data, which could be continuous, but of the ranks that the test calculates, and so of its U statistic and p-value. The test ranks all the observations from two groups and counts, for every pair made of one observation from each group, which group’s member ranks higher. The U statistic is that count.
Rank tests are a good target because they are used where samples are small and data are not normal: animal studies, pilot trials, and small clinical samples. These are the conditions under which granularity is coarse and the test can fail.
Hussey subsequently formalised an analytic form of GRIM-U, which does not need to enumerate every possible ranking, and implemented it in the {analyticgrimu} R package (Hussey, 2026). For the moment, this chapter does not attempt to explain analytic GRIM-U in any detail, or examine the sample sizes at which its results are informative, or consider the complexities of (assumed) maximum number of ties, etc. GRIM-U is still in early development; this content might be added later. Right now, the point is merely to highlight that other granularity methods do or could exist, and that this is an area of active research in methods development.

12.7.1 Additional assumptions
GRIM-U needs more assumptions than GRIM, because a Mann-Whitney p-value can be calculated in several ways. Software may use the exact distribution or a normal approximation, with or without a continuity correction, and with or without a correction for ties. Exact p-values are also defined in more than one way. Sidedness matters too. {analyticgrimu} treats these as GRIM treats rounding: a reported result passes if any modelled convention reproduces it.
Ties are the largest source of leniency. Ties shrink the variance of U, so the same U can give a range of p-values depending on how heavily tied the data were. The package computes that range exactly and accepts anything inside it, so a correctly reported result from tied data is never flagged. The price is that the default test is weak. Checking a p-value on its own will almost never flag anything, and detection is one-sided: a p-value that is too large for its U can be caught, but one that is too small can always be explained by supposing more ties.
Two features recover some of the lost ground. If the measure is known to be continuous, or to have a known number of scale points, this can be stated, and the accepted range narrows. The share of three-decimal p-values that are attainable for two groups of six falls from 94% when any ties are allowed to 7% when there are none.

grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3)

[1] 0.9380619

grimu_saturation(n1 = 6, n2 = 6, decimals = 3, ties = "none")

[1] 0.06993007


These options are safe in one direction only. If the data were more tied than was assumed, correct results will be flagged, so it is better to err towards allowing ties. The function also reports the minimum amount of tying that a consistent explanation would require. A result that is only possible if half the sample shares one value is unremarkable for a single five-point item and not credible for a reaction time.
One coverage gap remains. Some software computes an exact permutation p-value conditional on the observed pattern of ties, which cannot be reconstructed from the group sizes. A failure against a result produced that way may reflect the gap and not an error.
Heathers & Grimes (2025) demonstrate GRIM-U on four published medical studies. No large-scale applications of GRIM-U have been conducted to date.

title: 12  Granularity methods ✎ Draft
text:
12.8 Test yourself
Answer all the questions, then click the button below the quiz to see why each answer is right. Unless a question says otherwise, values are reported to two decimals, each participant answers a single question with a whole number, and halves may be rounded up or down.

What GRIM and GRIMMER are for

Forensic methods are often divided into tests of possibility and tests of plausibility. Which kind of test is GRIM? A possibility testA plausibility testBothNeither
GRIM checks whether a reported mean could have been produced by N whole-number scores. TRUEFALSE
GRIMMER can show that a reported SD is impossible even when the reported mean passes GRIM. TRUEFALSE
A GRIM failure shows that the authors fabricated their data. TRUEFALSE

A mean outside the scale. A study collects ratings from 10 participants on a 1–7 scale, and reports their mean as 12.10.

GRIM flags this mean as inconsistent. TRUEFALSE
This mean could have come from the data described. TRUEFALSE

Assumptions

A 12-item questionnaire is scored by adding up each participant’s answers. What number of items averaged should GRIM use? 112144It depends on the sample size
The same questionnaire is instead scored as the mean of the 12 items, in a sample of 15. GRIM can detect an error in the reported mean of these scores. TRUEFALSE
Estimated marginal means from an ANCOVA can be tested with GRIM, as long as the raw scores were whole numbers. TRUEFALSE
A mean of 3.12 from 8 participants is GRIM-consistent whichever way halves were rounded. TRUEFALSE

Sample size and informativeness

A mean age in years from 120 participants is reported to two decimals. GRIM can detect an error in this mean. TRUEFALSE
A mean from 90 participants passes GRIM. Roughly what share of two-decimal values picked at random would also pass? 10%50%90%100%
Because the mean from 90 participants passed GRIM, there is good evidence that it was reported correctly. TRUEFALSE
A mean from 12 participants that passes GRIM tells us more than a mean from 90 participants that passes GRIM. TRUEFALSE
With 150 participants, GRIMMER can still find an impossible SD even though GRIM can no longer fail. TRUEFALSE




Why is each answer right?


A possibility test. GRIM asks whether a reported mean can exist at all, given the sample size and whole-number data. It does not ask whether the result is surprising or unlikely, which is what plausibility tests do. See the chapter on organising principles.
True. That is the whole test: some whole-number sum, divided by N × items and rounded, must give the reported mean (Section 12.2).
True. GRIMMER adds a second check, on the sum of the squared scores, which must be a whole number with the same parity (odd or even) as the sum of the scores. An SD can fail this check even when the mean is fine (Section 12.3).
False. A failure shows that the mean, the sample size, the description of the measure, and the rounding cannot all be as stated. It does not say which one is wrong, or why. In the largest application of GRIM, the causes found were mundane: wrong sample sizes, spreadsheet errors, values copied incorrectly, and stepped rounding (Section 12.4).
False. 12.10 × 10 = 121, a whole number, so the mean is GRIM-consistent. GRIM only looks at the grid of attainable means. It knows nothing about the scale’s minimum and maximum.
False. On a 1–7 scale, no mean can be above 7. The value is impossible, but for a reason GRIM cannot see. Checks that use the scale’s limits are the subject of the next chapter, on bounds methods.
1. Each participant’s sum is a whole number, so a sum score behaves like a single item, however many items were added up. The number of items only enters the test when each participant’s answers are averaged first (Section 12.2.1).
False. With each participant’s score averaged over 12 items, the mean moves in steps of 1/(15 × 12) = 1/180. That is finer than the two-decimal reporting steps, so every two-decimal mean is attainable and the test cannot fail.
False. Model-based estimates such as estimated marginal means, covariate-adjusted means, and predicted values are not simple averages of the observed scores. Testing them with GRIM produces false positives (Table 12.3).
False. The only candidate sum is 25, and 25/8 = 3.125 exactly. Rounded half up, that is 3.13, so 3.12 fails. It passes only if halves can be rounded down, which is why the lenient rule counts it as consistent (Note 12.1).
False. With a single item and 100 or more participants, attainable means are no further apart than the reporting steps of 0.01, so every two-decimal mean passes. The test is uninformative here (Section 12.2.3).
90%. With two decimals and fewer than 100 participants on a single item, about N% of all printable values are attainable. So a value made up at random would pass 90% of the time (Section 12.2.2).
False. A test that 90% of random numbers would pass is weak evidence of anything. The pass is what we would expect if the mean were correct, and also very nearly what we would expect if it were not. A consistent result at large N should be read as “not shown to be impossible”, not as “shown to be correct” (Section 12.2.4).
True. At N = 12, a random value would pass only about 12% of the time, so a pass rules out more ways of being wrong. The informativeness of a pass depends on how often a wrong value would have failed.
True. GRIMMER’s check on the SD stays demanding at larger samples when the SD is small. For example, with a mean of 3.50 from 150 participants, 5 of the 21 two-decimal SDs from 0.40 to 0.60 are impossible, even though every two-decimal mean is attainable (Figure 12.4).

title: 13  Bounds methods ✎ Draft
text:
13.1 Mean inside range
The methods in this chapter rest on the properties of bounded data described in Chapter 7: on a scale with a minimum and a maximum, the mean and the SD are not free to take any values independently of one another.
The simplest bounds check is whether a mean lies within the range of values that its scores could take. The mean of a single item rated from 1 to 5 must lie between 1 and 5. The range of a sum score is the number of items multiplied by the lowest and highest response options, so six items rated from 1 to 5 give sum scores from 6 to 30, and their mean must lie between 6 and 30. A percentage must lie between 0 and 100. When an article reports the smallest and largest observed scores, the mean must also lie between those. And a mean exactly at the minimum or maximum is only possible if every participant had that score, in which case the SD must be zero (Section 7.2).
Working out the range requires knowing the number of items, the response options, how they were coded (for example, from 0 or from 1), and whether items were summed or averaged. Articles sometimes describe these inconsistently, so a mean outside the range shows that either the mean or the description of the measure is wrong, without saying which.
The same reasoning applies to the means of subgroups. When the subgroups together make up the whole sample, without overlap, the mean of the whole sample is a weighted average of the subgroup means, so it must lie between the smallest and the largest of them. The same is true of percentages.
Haller et al. (2022) reported the characteristics of 9,496 participants in their Table 1, both for the whole sample and for eight regions, whose sample sizes add up to 9,496. In the whole sample, 5.1% of participants were divorced, but the table reports 0.0% divorced in every one of the eight regions. Likewise, 5.5% of the whole sample lived with friends or roommates, but 0.0% in every region. A percentage for the whole sample cannot be larger than the percentages in all of the groups that make it up, so these rows of the table cannot be correct. The regression in the same article’s Table 5 includes being divorced and living with friends or roommates as predictors, with estimated coefficients, which suggests that participants in these groups did exist and that the regional zeros are the error.
The same article also describes the ranges of two of its measures inconsistently. The sum score of six prosocial behaviour items, each rated from 1 to 5, is described as ranging from 6 to 36 in the Method section, but from 6 to 30 in Table 4, which is correct. The fourteen well-being items are described as rated on a “6-point” scale from 0 to 6, which has seven points, while the range of the sum score is given as 0 to 70, which is only possible if each item was scored from 0 to 5. None of these means falls outside its range, but the inconsistencies show why the range of a measure should be worked out from its items, not taken from the article.

title: 13  Bounds methods ✎ Draft
13  Bounds methods ✎ Draft
13  Bounds methods ✎ Draft
text:
13.4 Coefficient bounds
Many coefficients have bounds that follow from how they are defined, whatever was measured. A correlation must lie between −1 and 1, and a proportion or an R2 between 0 and 1. Reliability, defined as the proportion of the variance in scores that is true-score variance, also lies between 0 and 1, but the coefficients used to estimate it are bounded less tightly. Cronbach’s α cannot exceed 1, but it has no lower bound: it is negative whenever the items are, on average, negatively correlated with one another, as happens when reverse-keyed items have not been reverse-scored, and two items that correlate −.90 give an α of −18. A negative α is therefore possible, but it shows that the items do not measure one thing in the way they were scored, and so it is a reason to look closely. A reported value outside a coefficient’s bounds cannot be correct. Table 13.1 lists the bounds of some statistics that are common in psychology and medicine.



Table 13.1: Bounds of some common statistics.










Statistic
Bounds
Notes




Pearson’s r, Spearman’s ρ, Kendall’s τ, point-biserial and phi correlations
−1 to 1
For phi and point-biserial correlations, the attainable maximum is often smaller, depending on the proportions in each category.


Proportions, probabilities, and p-values
0 to 1 (0% to 100%)
Includes prevalence, response rates, and proportions of variance.


Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score
0 to 1
All are proportions, and the F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it lies between them.


Area under the ROC curve (AUC, c-statistic)
0 to 1
0.5 is chance. Values below 0.5 mean that the predictor works in the opposite direction to the one assumed.


R2, η2, partial η2, Cramér’s V
0 to 1



Adjusted R2
−p / (n − p − 1) to 1, with p predictors
Can be slightly negative when R2 is close to zero: at least −0.03 with 3 predictors and 100 people. It is only substantially negative when there are many predictors for the sample size.


ω2 (one-way ANOVA)
−dfeffect / (N − dfeffect) to 1
Can be slightly negative when the effect is close to zero: at least −0.01 for two groups and 100 people. Often reported as 0 when negative.


ε2 (one-way ANOVA)
−dfeffect / dferror to 1
As for ω2: at least −0.01 for two groups of 50.


Standardised regression coefficients (β)
−1 to 1 with one predictor
With several correlated predictors, values beyond ±1 are possible, but rare, and worth a closer look.


Standardised factor loadings
−1 to 1
A value beyond ±1, known as a Heywood case, indicates an improper solution.


Cronbach’s α
Up to 1, with no lower bound
Negative when the items are on average negatively correlated, usually because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored. A slightly negative α is possible but a sign of a problem with the scale or its scoring. A value far below 0, such as −5, needs items that are strongly negatively correlated, which is implausible for a published scale unless the article explains it.


McDonald’s ω
0 to 1



Single-measure intraclass correlation (one-way, or two-way consistency)
−1 / (k − 1) to 1, with k raters or measurements per subject
−1 to 1 with two raters, and closer to 0 with more. Estimates are negative when the variance between subjects is close to zero, and are then usually only slightly negative. The two-way agreement form can fall slightly further below in very small samples.


Average-measure intraclass correlation
Up to 1, with no lower bound
The consistency form is identical to Cronbach’s α, and is negative under the same circumstances.


Cohen’s κ
−1 to 1
The attainable maximum is often below 1, depending on the marginal proportions.


Odds ratio, risk ratio, hazard ratio
Above 0
1 means no difference. Ratios cannot be zero or negative, so neither can the bounds of their intervals, although a small lower bound can be rounded to 0.00.


Risk difference
−1 to 1



Number needed to treat (NNT)
1 or more in size
An NNT between −1 and 1 would imply a risk difference greater than 1 in size.


Variances, SDs, and standard errors
0 or more
For a single mean, the standard error, SD / √N, cannot be larger than the SD.


I2
0% to 100%



τ2, χ2, F, RMSEA, SRMR
0 or more



CFI
0 to 1
The TLI is not bounded in the same way, and can fall below 0 or rise above 1.


Cohen’s d and other Standardized Mean Differences
No bounds by definition
On a bounded scale, the bounds of the scale limit how large a Standardized Mean Difference can be (Chapter 7).






Some of the statistics in Table 13.1 are bias-corrected or variance-based estimates that can legitimately fall slightly below zero when the quantity they estimate is close to zero, such as adjusted R2, ω2, and the intraclass correlation. Being able to fall slightly below zero does not mean that they have no bounds. Most of them have a lower bound that follows from the sample size or design, and it is usually close to zero. An R2 of −4.1 is impossible, because R2 cannot be negative at all, and an adjusted R2 that negative would need an R2 of zero and almost as many predictors as people. A single-measure intraclass correlation of −9.1 is also impossible in practice: the one-way and consistency forms cannot fall below −1 with any number of raters, and the agreement form can only do so in samples of a few subjects. Only a few statistics, such as Cronbach’s α and the average-measure intraclass correlation, have no lower bound at all, and even for these, a value far below zero is implausible without a specific explanation.
Values this obviously wrong still reach print. Hussein et al. (2022) compared machine learning models for classifying lung diseases from chest X-rays, and reported each model’s accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), so it must lie between them, and like them between 0 and 1. As a comment on PubPeer pointed out, every F1 score in the article’s Tables 2 to 4 is above 1, ranging from 1.40 to 3.64. They are not percentages, because the precision and recall in the same rows are reported as proportions. Almost all of them are four times the recall in the same row: one model was reported with a precision of .6900, a recall of .6891, and an F1 score of 2.7563, whereas the F1 score implied by its precision and recall is .6895. Whatever the cause, none of the F1 scores can be correct. Later comments on the same article raise further questions about the other metrics in these tables.
Errors like these are not rare. Bogdan (2025) extracted the statistics reported in thousands of published psychology articles. The resulting dataset contains 110,016 reported correlations, and 0.8% of them lie outside −1 to 1, so they cannot be correct.
Values that only break a bound once they are combined with other reported numbers are probably more common, because no one checks the combination. The next section describes one such check.

13.4.1 Disattenuated correlations
Measurement error weakens correlations. If two measures are not perfectly reliable, the correlation between them is smaller in size than the correlation between the constructs they measure, a bias known as attenuation. Spearman (1904) showed how to correct for it: divide the observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two measures’ reliabilities,
\[
r_{xy}^{\text{true}} = \frac{r_{xy}}{\sqrt{r_{xx} \, r_{yy}}},
\]
where rxy is the observed correlation and rxx and ryy are the reliabilities of the two measures, such as Cronbach’s α or a test–retest correlation. The disattenuated correlation is an estimate of the correlation between the constructs, and like any correlation it must lie between −1 and 1.
This gives a check that uses three numbers which articles often report together. Rearranging the formula, a correlation can only be as large as the square root of the product of the reliabilities: two measures with reliabilities of .70 can correlate at most .70, however closely related the constructs are. A reported correlation of .80 between them implies a disattenuated correlation of 1.14, which is impossible. Either the correlation, at least one of the reliabilities, or both are wrong, or the reliabilities were estimated in a different sample from the correlation.
Whether a disattenuated correlation outside −1 to 1 shows that the reported numbers are impossible, or only that they are implausible, depends on where the reliabilities come from. When the correlation and both reliabilities were estimated in the same sample, as when an article reports all three, they describe the same data, and the check is a possibility check: the numbers cannot all be correct, subject to the caveats about sampling error and the type of reliability below. When the reliabilities come from other samples, such as a test manual, earlier studies, or a meta-analysis, the check is a plausibility check. The reliabilities then describe what is typical for the measures, and the measures may have been more or less reliable in the sample at hand, so a disattenuated correlation outside −1 to 1 shows that the reported correlation is implausible given what is known about the measures, not that it is impossible. For the same reason, √(rxx ryy) is a ceiling on the correlation to be expected between two measures, not on the correlation that can be observed in any one sample, which varies around its expected value.
The plausibility check can be applied to meta-analyses as well as to single studies. Vahey et al. (2015) reported a meta-analytic correlation of r = .45 between the Implicit Relational Assessment Procedure (IRAP), a reaction-time-based measure, and clinical criterion measures. A later meta-analysis estimated the IRAP’s internal consistency at α = .27 and its test–retest reliability at .18 (Hussey & Drake, 2020). As Hussey (2025) pointed out, these estimates are incompatible with one another. Even if the criterion measures were assumed to be highly reliable (ryy = .90), the disattenuated correlation would be .91 using the IRAP’s internal consistency and 1.12 using its test–retest reliability. With a lower and arguably more plausible criterion reliability of .70, it would be 1.04 or 1.27. Either the meta-analytic correlation was too large, or the meta-analytic reliabilities were too small. A reanalysis of the original meta-analysis found serious errors that generally inflated the effect size, and a new meta-analysis calculated to show their combined impact produced an estimate half the size, r = .22 (Hussey, 2025).
Enter a reported correlation and the reliabilities of the two measures below, and choose whether the reliabilities come from the same sample as the correlation, which makes the check a possibility check, or from other samples, which makes it a plausibility check. The plot shows the reported correlation and the disattenuated correlation, joined by an arrow; the grey areas outside −1 and 1 are impossible for any correlation. You can also click or drag anywhere on the plot to set the reported correlation. The app uses the values exactly as entered and does not allow for their rounding, so it is better treated as an intuition pump than as a formal test.

viewof dcR = Inputs.number([-1, 1], {value: 0.20, step: 0.01, label: "Correlation (r_xy)"})
// reliability estimates such as alpha can be negative, so the reliability boxes accept any value up to 1
viewof dcRxx = Inputs.number([-Infinity, 1], {value: 0.70, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of measure 1 (r_xx)"})
viewof dcRyy = Inputs.number([-Infinity, 1], {value: 0.70, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability of measure 2 (r_yy)"})
// reliabilities from the same sample as the correlation make the check a possibility check; reliabilities from other
// samples make it a plausibility check
viewof dcSameSample = Inputs.radio(new Map([["The same sample as the correlation (possibility check)", true], ["Other samples, such as a test manual or meta-analysis (plausibility check)", false]]), {value: true, label: "Reliabilities from"})






























dcState = {
  // the inputs, checked: the correlation must be a number in [-1, 1], and the reliabilities numbers no greater than 1.
  // a reliability estimate of zero or below is possible for a coefficient such as alpha, but the correction cannot
  // be applied to it, because it takes the square root of the product of the reliabilities
  const r = dcR, rxx = dcRxx, ryy = dcRyy
  const finite = [r, rxx, ryy].every(Number.isFinite)
  if (!finite) return {error: "Enter the correlation and both reliabilities as numbers."}
  if (r < -1 || r > 1) return {error: "<strong>Not possible.</strong> The reported correlation is itself outside −1 to 1, so it cannot be correct whatever the reliabilities."}
  if (rxx > 1 || ryy > 1) return {error: "<strong>Not possible.</strong> No reliability coefficient can be greater than 1."}
  if (rxx <= 0 || ryy <= 0) return {error: `<strong>Cannot be corrected.</strong> A reliability of ${Math.min(rxx, ryy).toFixed(2).replace("-", "−")} is possible for an estimate such as Cronbach's α, but the correction for attenuation is only defined for reliabilities above 0. A reliability estimate at or below 0 means that the items do not hang together as scored, for example because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored, and is itself worth questioning.`, kind: "warn"}
  const ceiling = Math.sqrt(rxx * ryy)
  const dis = r / ceiling
  return {r, rxx, ryy, ceiling, dis, possible: Math.abs(dis) <= 1}
}







{
  if (dcState.error) {
    const box = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${dcState.kind ?? "bad"}">`
    box.innerHTML = dcState.error
    return box
  }
  const {r, rxx, ryy, ceiling, dis, possible} = dcState
  const same = dcSameSample
  const blue = "#2780e3", green = "#3b9c6e", red = "#c0392b", amber = "#d9a02b"
  // outside -1 to 1 is impossible when the reliabilities come from the same sample, and implausible when they do not
  const disColour = possible ? green : same ? red : amber
  const fmt = x => x.toFixed(2).replace("-", "−")

  const tiles = html`<div class="sb-tiles">
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: ${blue};">${fmt(r)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Reported <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">the observed correlation</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: ${disColour};">${fmt(dis)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Disattenuated <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">must lie between −1 and 1</div></div>
    <div><div class="sb-tile-value" style="color: inherit;">±${ceiling.toFixed(2)}</div><div class="sb-tile-label">Reliability ceiling on <i>r</i></div><div class="sb-tile-note">√(<i>r<sub>xx</sub></i> × <i>r<sub>yy</sub></i>): the largest correlation to expect with these reliabilities, not a limit on what any one sample can show</div></div>
  </div>`

  // the axis always shows -1 to 1, and stretches to show a disattenuated correlation beyond them
  const span = Math.max(1.25, Math.abs(dis) * 1.12)
  const points = [
    {x: r, label: "reported", colour: blue},
    {x: dis, label: "disattenuated", colour: disColour}
  ]
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width, height: 190, marginLeft: 20, marginRight: 20, marginTop: 10, marginBottom: 40,
    x: {label: "Correlation", labelAnchor: "center", labelOffset: 34, domain: [-span, span], ticks: d3.ticks(-span, span, 10)},
    y: {axis: null, domain: [0, 1]},
    style: {fontSize: "13px"},
    marks: [
      // outside -1 to 1: impossible for any correlation
      Plot.rect([{x1: -span, x2: -1}, {x1: 1, x2: span}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: 1, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.08}),
      Plot.ruleX([-1, 1], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
      Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
      // the labels of the grey areas sit at the bottom, below the disattenuated correlation's labels, which can be
      // inside them
      Plot.text(["Impossible"], {x: 1 + (span - 1) / 2, y: 0.03, fontWeight: 600, fillOpacity: 0.6, lineAnchor: "bottom"}),
      Plot.text(["Impossible"], {x: -1 - (span - 1) / 2, y: 0.03, fontWeight: 600, fillOpacity: 0.6, lineAnchor: "bottom"}),
      Math.abs(dis - r) > 1e-9 ? Plot.arrow([{}], {x1: r, x2: dis, y1: 0.5, y2: 0.5, stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.6, strokeWidth: 1.5, insetEnd: 8, headLength: 10}) : null,
      Plot.dot(points, {x: "x", y: 0.5, r: 7, fill: "colour", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
      // the reported correlation is labelled below its point and the disattenuated correlation above, so that the
      // labels do not overlap when the two are close together
      Plot.text([points[0]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: d => fmt(d.x), dy: 17, fill: "colour", fontWeight: 700}),
      Plot.text([points[0]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: "label", dy: 32, fill: "colour"}),
      Plot.text([points[1]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: d => fmt(d.x), dy: -16, fill: "colour", fontWeight: 700}),
      Plot.text([points[1]], {x: "x", y: 0.5, text: "label", dy: -31, fill: "colour"})
    ]
  })
  // clicking the plot sets the reported correlation to the clicked value, and dragging moves it continuously. the
  // plot is redrawn at every change, and its axis can stretch as the disattenuated correlation grows, so the drag is
  // followed on the window and positions are converted with the latest plot's scale
  dcDrag.scale = plot.scale("x")
  plot.style.cursor = "crosshair"
  plot.style.touchAction = "none"
  plot.addEventListener("pointerdown", down => {
    const box = plot.getBoundingClientRect()
    const setR = event => {
      const value = dcDrag.scale.invert((event.clientX - box.left) * width / box.width)
      viewof dcR.value = Math.max(-1, Math.min(1, Math.round(value * 100) / 100))
      viewof dcR.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
    }
    down.preventDefault()
    setR(down)
    let pending = null
    const move = event => {
      if (pending === null) requestAnimationFrame(() => { setR(pending); pending = null })
      pending = event
    }
    const up = () => {
      window.removeEventListener("pointermove", move)
      window.removeEventListener("pointerup", up)
      window.removeEventListener("pointercancel", up)
    }
    window.addEventListener("pointermove", move)
    window.addEventListener("pointerup", up)
    window.addEventListener("pointercancel", up)
  })

  // the smallest reliability each measure could have, given the other one, for the disattenuated correlation to be
  // within -1 to 1
  const minRxx = r * r / ryy, minRyy = r * r / rxx
  const needed = (min, name, other) => min > 1 ? `with measure ${other}'s reliability as ${same ? "reported" : "given"}, no reliability of measure ${name} could bring it within −1 to 1` : `with measure ${other}'s reliability as ${same ? "reported" : "given"}, measure ${name} would need a reliability of at least ${min.toFixed(2)}`
  const [kind, message] = possible
    ? ["ok", same
      ? `<strong>Possible.</strong> Correcting for unreliability changes the correlation from ${fmt(r)} to ${fmt(dis)}, which is within −1 to 1.`
      : `<strong>Plausible.</strong> Correcting for unreliability changes the correlation from ${fmt(r)} to ${fmt(dis)}, which is within −1 to 1. With these typical reliabilities, correlations up to about ${ceiling.toFixed(2)} in size are to be expected.`]
    : same
      ? ["bad", `<strong>Not possible.</strong> The disattenuated correlation is ${fmt(dis)}, outside −1 to 1, so the reported correlation and reliabilities cannot all be correct for the same sample. For a correlation of ${fmt(r)}, the product of the reliabilities must be at least ${(r * r).toFixed(2)}: ${needed(minRxx, 1, 2)}; ${needed(minRyy, 2, 1)}.`]
      : ["warn", `<strong>Implausible.</strong> The disattenuated correlation is ${fmt(dis)}, outside −1 to 1. Because the reliabilities come from other samples, this does not show that the reported correlation is impossible: it would require the measures to have been more reliable in this sample than is typical for them. For a correlation of ${fmt(r)}, the product of the reliabilities in this sample must be at least ${(r * r).toFixed(2)}: ${needed(minRxx, 1, 2)}; ${needed(minRyy, 2, 1)}.`]
  const feedback = html`<div class="sb-feedback sb-feedback-${kind}">`
  feedback.innerHTML = message
  const note = html`<div class="dc-note">The values are used exactly as entered, without allowing for rounding, so treat the result as an intuition pump rather than a formal test.</div>`
  return html`${tiles}${plot}${feedback}${note}`
}

  .sb-feedback-ok { border-color: #3b9c6e; }
  .sb-feedback-warn { border-color: #d9a02b; }
  .sb-feedback-bad { border-color: #c0392b; }

Try a correlation of .80 with both reliabilities at .70: the disattenuated correlation is 1.14. Then raise either reliability until the correlation becomes possible. Negative correlations work the same way, against the lower bound of −1.
Some points to keep in mind when using this check:

Reliabilities from other samples are still informative. When an article does not report reliabilities, estimates from a test manual, earlier studies, or a reliability generalization meta-analysis can stand in for them, and the check becomes a plausibility check. It is often said that reliability is a property of scores in a particular sample rather than of a measure, but this is too strong. Reliability generalization meta-analyses, which pool the reliabilities reported for a measure across many samples, find that reliability varies between samples but that the measure itself also contributes to it (Vacha-Haase, 1998): some measures are reliable in most of the samples in which they are used, and others rarely are. A correlation that would be impossible given a measure’s typical reliability is not proof of an error, but it is a useful intuition pump and a fair reason to ask questions.
Small excesses can arise from sampling error. The correlation and the reliabilities are all estimates, and in small samples a disattenuated correlation slightly above 1 can occur by chance even when every reported number is correct. A disattenuated correlation of 1.02 in a sample of 50 is weak evidence of a problem. One of 1.30 in a sample of 500 is strong evidence.
Rounding is not taken into account. The app uses the values exactly as entered. A disattenuated correlation just above 1, calculated from values rounded to two decimal places, may be within rounding of a possible one, so the app is better treated as an intuition pump than as a formal test.
The type of reliability matters. Internal consistency coefficients such as Cronbach’s α can underestimate or overestimate reliability, depending on whether their assumptions hold, which changes the disattenuated correlation in turn. When an article reports more than one kind of reliability, check the result with each.
A disattenuated correlation close to 1 is itself informative. Even when it is possible, a disattenuated correlation near 1 suggests that the two measures assess the same construct, which may sit uneasily with an article’s claim that they measure distinct things.

title: 13  Bounds methods ✎ Draft
text:
13.5 Test yourself
Answer all the questions, then click the button below the quiz to see why each answer is right.

Means and SDs

A sum score of six items, each rated from 1 to 5, can range from 6 to 30. TRUEFALSE
When subgroups together make up a whole sample, the mean of the whole sample must lie between the smallest and largest subgroup means. TRUEFALSE
A table reports that 5.1% of a sample were divorced, and 0.0% in every one of the regions that make up the sample. This is possible if some of the regions are small. TRUEFALSE
If the mean of a single item rated from 1 to 5 is exactly 5, the SD must be 0. TRUEFALSE
On a 1–7 scale with 30 people, an SD of 3.20 is: Impossible, whatever the meanPossible only if the mean is 4Possible at any meanPossible only for whole-number data
At a given mean on a bounded scale, the largest possible SD is reached when: As many scores as possible are at the two ends of the scaleThe scores are spread evenly across the scaleThe scores are bunched around the meanHalf the scores are equal to the mean
With whole-number responses, a mean of 2.97 can have an SD of 0. TRUEFALSE
A reported minimum and maximum can make a small SD impossible, even though the same SD would be possible if only the scale limits were known. TRUEFALSE
A reported Cronbach’s α can make a large SD impossible, even though the same SD would be possible without it. TRUEFALSE
A reported SD that lies within the BRIMMER bounds has been shown to be possible. TRUEFALSE
An SD above the uniform-spread bound is impossible. TRUEFALSE
With a small sample on a short scale, a reported mean and SD can be enough to recover every individual score. TRUEFALSE

Estimates inside confidence intervals

An estimate that lies outside its own 95% confidence interval is: Almost always an errorCommon when intervals are bootstrappedExpected for odds ratiosA sign of p-hacking
Among ratios reported with confidence intervals in MEDLINE abstracts, roughly what share were outside their own intervals? Less than 1%About 5%About 15%None
An odds ratio should lie halfway between the lower and upper bounds of its confidence interval. TRUEFALSE
An estimate that is inside its interval but not in the middle of it, after allowing for rounding, is proof of an error. TRUEFALSE
Why should values be entered into the confidence interval app with their trailing zeros? The number of decimal places sets how much rounding is allowed forThe app cannot read numbers without themTrailing zeros show that the values are exactValues without them are treated as percentages
If swapping each estimate with its lower bound puts every estimate in the middle of its interval, the article’s values can be used as reported. TRUEFALSE

Coefficients

An article reports an F1 score of 2.76, alongside a precision of .69 and a recall of .69. The F1 score could be correct. TRUEFALSE
An adjusted R2 slightly below zero can be correct. TRUEFALSE
An ordinary R2 can be negative when a model fits very badly. TRUEFALSE
Cronbach’s α can be negative. TRUEFALSE
The standard error of a single mean can be larger than the SD. TRUEFALSE
Two measures each have a reliability of .70. What is the largest correlation to expect between them? .70.49.841.00
An article reports a correlation and the reliabilities of both measures, all estimated in its own sample, which give a disattenuated correlation of 1.14. This is a possibility check rather than a plausibility check. TRUEFALSE
A correlation of .80 is reported between two measures whose reliabilities, taken from their test manuals, are both .70. This shows that the correlation is impossible. TRUEFALSE




Why is each answer right?


True. The range of a sum score is the number of items times the lowest and highest response options: 6 × 1 = 6 and 6 × 5 = 30. Work the range out from the items rather than taking it from the article, which may describe it inconsistently (Section 13.1).
True. The mean of the whole sample is a weighted average of the subgroup means, so it cannot be smaller than all of them or larger than all of them. The same is true of percentages (Section 13.1).
False. However small or large the regions are, a percentage for the whole sample cannot be larger than the percentages in every one of the groups that make it up. If every region has 0.0%, so must the whole sample (Section 13.1).
True. A mean exactly at the maximum is only possible if every participant had the maximum score, and then there is no spread at all (Section 13.1).
Impossible, whatever the mean. With 30 people on a 1–7 scale, no SD can exceed 3.05, which is reached with half the people at each end of the scale (Section 13.2).
As many scores as possible are at the two ends of the scale. The most spread out samples have their scores at the two ends, with at most one person in between. Moving the mean away from the middle of the scale lowers this ceiling (Section 13.2).
False. An SD of 0 means that everyone had the same score, and identical whole numbers cannot have a mean with a fractional part, such as 2.97. Whole-number data raise the floor above zero at every mean that is not a whole number (Section 13.2).
True. A sample that includes both the observed minimum and the observed maximum cannot have a very small SD. On a 1–7 scale with 30 people and a mean of 2.97, reporting a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 6 raises the floor from 0.14 to 0.71 (Section 13.2).
True. A reported α limits how much the items can disagree with one another, which lowers the ceiling on the SD of the total or mean score (Section 13.2).
False. BRIMMER is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. A reported SD inside the bounds may still not correspond to any real set of whole-number scores; only BRIMMEST settles that (Section 13.2, Chapter 14).
False. The uniform-spread bound is a bound on what is plausible, not on what is possible. Above it, the scores are more spread out than if they were spread evenly across the whole scale, which requires them to pile up at its ends. That is plausible for some measures, but not most (Section 13.2).
True. In a small sample on a short scale, many combinations of mean and SD are produced by only one set of whole-number scores, so the mean and SD alone reveal every score (Section 13.2).
Almost always an error. For almost every method used in practice, a confidence interval contains its own estimate. The exceptions are rare, and an article that used one would be expected to say so (Section 13.3.1).
Less than 1%. Between 0.4% and 0.6% of ratios, depending on the type, were outside their intervals, and 0.43% once rounding was taken into account. The share is small, but almost every one points to an error (Section 13.3.1).
False. Intervals for ratios are usually calculated on the log scale, so the estimate lies halfway between the bounds on that scale: it is the geometric mean of the bounds, not their arithmetic mean (Section 13.3.2).
False. Many legitimate methods produce asymmetric intervals, such as profile likelihood, exact, Wilson, and bootstrap intervals. Whether an off-centre estimate is a concern depends on the metric and on the method the article used (Section 13.3.2).
The number of decimal places sets how much rounding is allowed for. A bound reported as 0.30 could have been anything from 0.295 to 0.305, but one entered as 0.3 could have been anything from 0.25 to 0.35 (Section 13.3).
False. Even if the columns were simply swapped, readers and meta-analysts usually take reported values at face value, and a meta-analyst who uses the wrong estimate or calculates the wrong standard error will distort the pooled results (Section 13.3).
False. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it must lie between them, and like them between 0 and 1. With a precision and recall of .69, the F1 score is .69 (Section 13.4).
True. Adjusted R2 is bias-corrected, and can fall slightly below zero when R2 is close to zero. Its lower bound depends on the number of predictors and the sample size, and is usually close to zero (Section 13.4).
False. R2 is a proportion of variance, so it lies between 0 and 1. A reported R2 below zero cannot be correct (Section 13.4).
True. Cronbach’s α has no lower bound, and is negative when the items are on average negatively correlated, usually because reverse-keyed items were not reverse-scored. A negative α is possible, but a sign of a problem with the scale or its scoring (Section 13.4).
False. The standard error of a single mean is SD / √N, so it cannot be larger than the SD (Section 13.4).
.70. The largest correlation to expect is the square root of the product of the reliabilities: √(.70 × .70) = .70, however closely related the constructs are (Section 13.4.1).
True. When the correlation and both reliabilities describe the same data, they cannot all be correct if the disattenuated correlation is outside −1 to 1, subject to sampling error, rounding, and the type of reliability used (Section 13.4.1).
False. The disattenuated correlation would be 1.14, but because the reliabilities come from other samples, this is a plausibility check, not a possibility check: the measures may have been more reliable in this sample. It is a good reason to ask questions, but not proof of an error (Section 13.4.1).

title: 14  Combined granularity and bounds methods ✎ Draft
text:
14.1 Granularity and bounds are different questions
Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 describe two families of checks on reported means and SDs. Granularity checks ask whether a reported value can be produced by whole-number data at all: GRIM for the mean and GRIMMER for the SD. Bounds checks ask whether a reported value lies within the range that the scale and the other reported values allow: BRIM for the mean and BRIMMER for the SD (Hussey et al., 2026). The two families divide along two axes, the statistic being checked and the kind of constraint used, which gives four tests.
This chapter is about using the two families together. They answer different questions, so a reported mean and SD can pass one family and fail the other, and checking both rules out many more impossible values than checking either one alone. Even together they are necessary rather than sufficient conditions, and a fifth test, BRIMMEST, settles exactly whether any set of whole-number scores has the reported mean and SD.
Granularity and bounds are not nested, with one a stricter version of the other. They are orthogonal: each can pass or fail independently of the other (Hussey et al., 2026). GRIMMER asks whether the reported SD lies on the lattice of values that whole-number data can produce: the sum of the squared scores must be a whole number, with the same parity, odd or even, as the sum of the scores. It does not ask how large or small that SD is relative to the scale. BRIMMER asks only about magnitude: whether the SD lies between the smallest and largest values that the scale, the sample size, and the mean allow. It does not ask whether the SD lies on the lattice.
Three examples, all for five people answering a single item on a 1–5 scale, with means and SDs reported to two decimal places, show the possibilities:
The last example is why Hussey et al. (2026) add an exact test, BRIMMEST. For whole-number data, it works out every combination of mean and SD, after rounding, that some sample of whole-number scores on the scale can produce, and checks whether the reported pair is one of them. Unlike the other tests, passing BRIMMEST proves that a report is possible, rather than only failing to rule it out. It gives the same answer as the CLOSURE algorithm, which reconstructs every possible data set, but without reconstructing them.

title: 14  Combined granularity and bounds methods ✎ Draft
text:
A mean of 3.00 and an SD of 2.12 passes GRIM and GRIMMER, but fails BRIMMER. Five whole numbers with a mean of 3 can have a sum of squares that gives an SD of 2.12, so GRIMMER is satisfied. But no five scores between 1 and 5 with a mean of 3 can have an SD above 2.00, which is reached by two scores of 1, one of 3, and two of 5. GRIMMER does not know the scale’s limits, so it cannot see this.
A mean of 3.00 and an SD of 1.50 passes BRIMMER, but fails GRIMMER. An SD of 1.50 is comfortably within the bounds of 0 to 2.00, but the sum of squares it implies is even, whereas the sum of five scores with a mean of 3 is odd, so no whole-number data can produce it.
A mean of 3.00 and an SD of 1.73 passes GRIM, GRIMMER, and BRIMMER, but is still impossible. The squared deviations from the mean would have to add up to 12, and no five whole numbers between 1 and 5 with a mean of 3 have deviations whose squares add up to 12. All of the tests are necessary conditions, and none of them is sufficient.

text:
14.4 Test yourself
Answer all the questions, then click the button below the quiz to see why each answer is right.

Granularity and bounds

GRIM and BRIM both check the reported mean, but GRIM asks whether whole-number data can produce it, and BRIM asks whether it lies within the range that is possible. TRUEFALSE
A reported mean and SD that pass GRIMMER must also pass BRIMMER. TRUEFALSE
A reported mean and SD that pass BRIMMER must also pass GRIMMER. TRUEFALSE
Five people answer a single item on a 1–5 scale, and the article reports a mean of 3.00 and an SD of 2.12. Which check rules this out? BRIMMERGRIMGRIMMERNone of them
For the same design, a mean of 3.00 and an SD of 1.50. Which check rules this out? GRIMMERGRIMBRIMMERNone of them
For the same design, a mean of 3.00 and an SD of 1.73 passes GRIM, GRIMMER, and BRIMMER, so it is possible. TRUEFALSE
GRIMMER can accept SDs that are larger than any data on the scale can produce, because it does not use the scale’s limits. TRUEFALSE
Eight people report a mean of 1.50 and an SD of 0.00. This passes GRIMMER, but is impossible. TRUEFALSE
With five people, GRIMMER happens to reject every SD below the floor, but with larger samples it accepts some SDs below the floor. TRUEFALSE

Using the checks together

Passing BRIMMEST shows that some sample of whole-number scores on the scale has the reported mean and SD, after rounding. TRUEFALSE
A report that passes GRIM, GRIMMER, BRIM, and BRIMMER has been shown to be possible. TRUEFALSE
BRIMMEST works by reconstructing every possible data set, as CLOSURE does. TRUEFALSE
For five people on a 1–5 scale, roughly what share of the reported pairs that pass GRIM and GRIMMER fail BRIMMER? About 40%Almost noneAbout 5%All of them
The share of reports ruled out by each check is roughly the same for any scale and sample size. TRUEFALSE
With 100 or more people answering a single item, every mean reported to two decimal places passes GRIM. TRUEFALSE
When GRIM can no longer rule anything out, the bounds checks become: Relatively more importantUnnecessaryImpossible to applyIdentical to GRIMMER

Using the app

Why does the app default to quasi-integer rather than integer responses? It never rules out what integer data could produceIt allows responses such as 2.5It ignores the scale limitsIt makes BRIMMEST unnecessary
When both a Cronbach’s α and an observed minimum and maximum are entered, the app takes the higher of the two floors and the lower of the two ceilings. These bounds are valid, but may not be as sharp as possible. TRUEFALSE
Thirty people on a 1–7 scale report a mean of 2.97 and an SD of 2.83, which is close to the ceiling. This report is possible. TRUEFALSE




Why is each answer right?


True. The two families divide along two axes: the statistic being checked, and the kind of constraint. GRIM checks the mean’s granularity, and BRIM checks its range (Chapter 14).
False. GRIMMER only asks whether the SD lies on the lattice of values that whole-number data can produce. It does not ask how large or small the SD is relative to the scale, so it accepts many SDs that the bounds rule out (Section 14.1).
False. BRIMMER only asks about magnitude. An SD comfortably within the bounds can still be one that no whole-number data can produce (Section 14.1).
BRIMMER. Five whole numbers with a mean of 3 can have a sum of squares that gives an SD of 2.12, so GRIM and GRIMMER pass. But no five scores between 1 and 5 with a mean of 3 can have an SD above 2.00 (Section 14.1).
GRIMMER. An SD of 1.50 is within the bounds of 0 to 2.00, but the sum of squares it implies is even, whereas the sum of five scores with a mean of 3 is odd, so no whole-number data can produce it (Section 14.1).
False. The squared deviations from the mean would have to add up to 12, and no five whole numbers between 1 and 5 with a mean of 3 have deviations whose squares add up to 12. All of these tests are necessary conditions, and none is sufficient (Section 14.1).
True. With five people on a 1–5 scale, all of the reports that pass GRIM and GRIMMER but fail BRIMMER lie above the ceiling, and GRIM and GRIMMER also accept many reports beyond the ends of the scale (Section 14.2).
True. The sum of squares it implies, 18, is a whole number with the same parity as the sum of the scores, 12, so GRIMMER passes. But an SD of zero means that everyone had the same score, and eight identical whole numbers cannot have a mean of 1.50. Only the floor rules it out (Section 14.2).
True. GRIMMER does not check the floor. With five people its lattice is sparse at small SDs, so the smallest SD it accepts happens to equal the floor. With larger samples the lattice is denser, and it accepts SDs below the floor (Section 14.2).
True. Unlike the other checks, passing BRIMMEST proves that a report is possible, rather than only failing to rule it out (Section 14.1).
False. All four are necessary conditions. Some reports pass every one of them and still correspond to no real set of whole-number scores; only BRIMMEST settles that (Section 14.1).
False. BRIMMEST gives the same answer as CLOSURE, but without reconstructing the data sets: it works out which combinations of mean and SD, after rounding, whole-number samples on the scale can produce (Section 14.1).
About 40%. Of the 210 reported pairs that pass GRIM and GRIMMER, 89, or 42%, fail BRIMMER (Section 14.2).
False. The counts depend on the scale, the sample size, and the reporting precision. What generalises is the pattern: each check rules out reports that the others let through (Section 14.2).
True. Once the number of people times the number of items reaches 100, the possible means are no further apart than the 0.01 reporting step, so every two-decimal mean can be produced (Section 14.2).
Relatively more important. When granularity can no longer rule out any mean, the bounds carry more of the burden of detecting impossible values (Section 14.2).
It never rules out what integer data could produce. Quasi-integer gives a floor that is defined at every mean. It relaxes the whole-number requirement by one response, which makes the floor slightly more lenient, so it errs on the side of not flagging a possible report (Section 14.3).
True. {strait} has no joint bounds for α and observed extremes, so the app combines the two sets of bounds. Every report they rule out is impossible, but some impossible reports may slip through (Section 14.3).
True. Twenty people answering 1, nine answering 7, and one answering 6 give exactly these values (Section 14.3).
