title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
text:
16.1 Types of post-publication notice
Publication is not the end of an article’s history. After an article is published, its journal can correct it, warn readers about it, or retract it. These post-publication notices are the simplest thing to check in any trustworthiness assessment, and the first: they are checks 1.1 and 1.2 of INSPECT-SR (Section 24.2). A retracted article should usually not be relied on at all, whatever its methods and results look like.
This chapter explains what each kind of notice means, who decides to issue one, what a notice can and cannot tell you, and how to find them. The last of these is harder than it should be.
The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) is an organisation whose members include most major journals and publishers. Its guidelines are the closest thing to a standard for how journals handle problems with published articles, although they are advice rather than rules, and journals follow them unevenly. COPE describes three main kinds of notice, in increasing order of seriousness.

title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
text:
16.1.1 Corrections
A correction (sometimes called an erratum when the error was the publisher’s, or a corrigendum when it was the authors’) fixes an error in an article that is otherwise reliable: a wrong number in a table, a mislabelled figure, a missing funding statement. The article stays in the literature, and the correction is published as a separate notice linked to it. Many articles have corrections, and most are minor. But read them: a correction that changes a main result, or a series of corrections to the same article, can be a concern in itself.


16.1.2 Expressions of concern
An expression of concern warns readers that there are serious, credible doubts about an article’s reliability, but that the journal cannot yet decide whether to correct or retract it (COPE Council, 2025a). Typical reasons are that an investigation by the authors’ institution is still ongoing, that the journal is waiting for the authors to provide information such as their data, or that the authors have refused to provide it. An expression of concern can be a temporary notice, later replaced by a correction or a retraction, or it can be the final outcome if the case is never resolved. For a trustworthiness assessment, it is a strong warning: the journal itself is saying that the results may not be reliable.
In practice, journals rarely use them. Grey et al. (2026) extracted all the expressions of concern and retractions in the Retraction Watch Database up to the end of 2024.

3.3%
of retracted articles had been given an expression of concern before they were retracted (Grey et al., 2026).

Even among authors with more than five retractions, only 35% had any expression of concern on any of their articles. For most retracted articles, then, readers received no warning while the journal investigated, which can take years (Nature, 2014). Throughout that time the articles looked like any other published article and continued to be read, cited, and included in systematic reviews. The absence of an expression of concern therefore says very little about whether a journal has concerns about an article.


16.1.3 Retractions
A retraction is the most serious notice. It tells readers that the article’s findings and conclusions cannot be relied on (COPE Council, 2025b). Retraction is often described as “unpublishing” an article, but the article does not usually disappear. It normally stays online, marked as retracted (often with a “RETRACTED” watermark on every page) and linked to a retraction notice that explains, in principle, why. This keeps the record intact, so that readers who come across the article, or across citations of it, can find out that it has been retracted. Only rarely is an article removed entirely, for example for legal reasons or because following it could put people’s health at risk.
A retraction does not necessarily mean misconduct. COPE’s guidelines describe retraction as a way to correct the literature, not to punish the authors, and unreliable findings can come from honest error as well as from fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, or paper mills. Some retractions are requested by the authors themselves after they find a serious mistake. For a trustworthiness assessment this distinction matters less than it might seem: either way, the article’s results should not be used.
Retracted articles continue to be cited, often without any sign that the citing authors know about the retraction. This is easy to do. Most researchers have little reason to check whether an article they already know has been retracted, or to revisit its page on the publisher’s website, which is usually the only place the retraction is shown. Once an article is in your reference manager, nothing in a typical workflow removes it from the articles you can cite, so it can be cited for years after its retraction. Zotero helps with this: since 2019, it flags retracted articles in your library, shows the details of the retraction, and warns you if you try to cite one, or if a document already cites one that is later retracted (Stillman, 2019). It does this by checking the DOIs and PubMed IDs in your library against the Retraction Watch Database, the same database used by the checker in Section 16.6, without sending your library to Zotero’s servers. For this reason, I recommend Zotero as a reference manager.
Section 17.4 covers how to check an article’s references for retracted work.

title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
text:
16.2 Who decides?
Under COPE’s guidelines, the decision to correct, issue an expression of concern about, or retract an article belongs to the journal’s editor, because the editor is responsible for the journal’s content (COPE Council, 2025b). The publisher can support the editor, advise on how to handle a case, and issue the notice jointly, but should not make the decision, so that commercial interests do not influence it. While many (but not all) journals are COPE signatories, there is still a great deal of heterogeneity in processes. This may be due in part to editors not being aware of their own power. For example, editors sometimes ask authors’ institution to investigate, or defer to publisher’s research integrity offices. Institutional investigations can take years, some never happen or are never reported, and many people feel that they suffer from an inherent conflict of interest (e.g., an institution has an incentive to minimise reputation damage due to its employees behavior). Different entities also make judgement about different things: COPE states that an editors role is to retract if they have lost confidence in the work, not to adjuicate whether research integrity violations took place. These are often conflated - for example, sufficient ambiguity can lead to an editor losing confidence in a specific article, even if there is not sufficient evidence for a university research integrity committee to assert that research misconduct occurred. The point of this section is not to overly editorialise about who should make a decision here, only to note that despite clarity about who can make a decision, about what, on what timeline, and in conjunction with what other entities.
The result is that notices are slow, and their absence means little. Many articles with serious problems have no notice at all, and many that are eventually retracted were cited for years before the retraction.

title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
section: 16.3 What retraction notices do and do not tell you
text:
16.3 What retraction notices do and do not tell you
A retraction notice is not a full account of what happened and should not be read as one. It is the most conservative statement the journal is confident it can defend - possibly in court.
Notices are often (partially) negotiated with the authors, and checked by the publisher’s lawyers before they are published. Because an author who is named in a notice as having committed misconduct may sue, this is rarely stated outright. In a 2014 editorial, Nature explained that “for legal reasons” it could not usually use retraction statements to highlight wrongdoing (Nature, 2014). The result is notices that say little: that “concerns were raised about the data”, that the editor “no longer has confidence in the findings”, or that the authors “could not provide the raw data”. In an analysis of 7,318 retraction notices, 73.7% did not say whether any institutional investigation had led to the retraction (Xu et al., 2023).
Notices can also show signs of negotiation directly. The retraction notice for the article described in Section 17.1 ends by stating that the author “agrees with this retraction but for different reasons than those stated here” (American Psychological Association, 2026).
So a notice that does not mention misconduct is not evidence that there was none, and a vague reason such as “error” may cover anything from a typo to fabrication. For more context, look for other sources: PubPeer comments, coverage by Retraction Watch, and published reports of institutional investigations. For a trustworthiness assessment, though, what matters most is usually the fact of the retraction rather than its stated reason. A retraction for any reason means the article’s results should not be used, and a retraction for misconduct also raises questions about the authors’ other work (INSPECT-SR check 1.3).
Relatedly, whereas there is a normative requirement in science that authors of research be given fair credit by being named as authors of articles, there is no comparable norm in retraction notices to give fair credit to the people who detected the problems. Most notices mention that issues were raised by “a reader”, for example, but not by name. While I understand there may be legal reasons for doing so, this contributes to the perverse incentive structures in science.

title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
section: 16.4 There is no single database of retractions
text:
16.4 There is no single database of retractions
It would be reasonable to expect a single, complete list of retracted articles. Surprisingly, there is none. Retractions are recorded in several places, and they often disagree.
Publishers are supposed to register notices with Crossref, the organisation that registers the DOIs of most journal articles, but many do not, or do so incompletely. PubMed and commercial indexes such as Web of Science and Scopus each record retractions in their own way, for the journals they cover. The Retraction Watch Database, compiled by hand by Retraction Watch from publishers’ websites and other sources, is the most comprehensive, and Crossref acquired it in 2023 and now makes it openly available.
Schneider et al. (2023) combined the retractions recorded by Crossref, the Retraction Watch Database, Scopus, and Web of Science, giving 49,924 publications that at least one source recorded as retracted.

3%
of publications recorded as retracted by at least one of four major sources were recorded as retracted by all four (Schneider et al., 2023).

For almost 30% of the publications, one source recorded a retraction that another, which indexed the same publication, did not. Of the retracted publications that Scopus indexed, it failed to mark 32% as retracted, compared with 7% for Crossref and 4% for Web of Science.
The practical consequence is that checking one source is not enough. The checker below therefore combines four:

notices that publishers have registered with Crossref;
the Retraction Watch Database, which Crossref now includes alongside the publishers’ own records;
PubMed, which links articles to retraction notices and expressions of concern, and tags retracted articles;
the article’s title, because some publishers mark a retraction only by changing the title (e.g., “RETRACTED: …”).

This approach follows, and was inspired by, the “Annulled” and “Concerning” detectors of the Problematic Paper Screener (Cabanac et al., 2022), which combine the same sources. The difference is that this checker queries the sources live, whereas the Problematic Paper Screener’s lists are updated periodically.

title: 16  Inspecting post-publication notices ✎ Draft
text:
16.5 PubPeer and its browser extension
Formal notices are only part of an article’s post-publication history. PubPeer is a website where anyone can comment on published articles, and it has become the main place where problems with articles are reported and discussed. Comments are moderated, may be posted anonymously, and are often detailed: they report duplicated or manipulated images, impossible statistics, inconsistencies with the trial registration, nonexistent references, and the other problems covered in this book. Authors can reply, and commenters often post updates when a correction, expression of concern, or retraction is published, as in the example in Section 17.1. Because journals are slow to act, and because most retractions are not preceded by an expression of concern, a PubPeer thread is often the first, and sometimes the only, public sign that an article has problems.
PubPeer comments are not verdicts. Read the thread, check the claims it makes, and treat it as information to assess and verify, not as a conclusion. When reading and writing PubPeer comments, remember that a good comment is one that provides verifiable information that might adjust our trust in the work.
Many of the arguments made against PubPeer are straw men that neglect the principled reasons it works the way it does.
Some argue that PubPeer comments are not legitimate because they have not been peer reviewed, although PubPeer has never claimed that they are. Its moderators check comments against its rules, not their scientific merit, and readers are expected to judge each comment on the evidence it presents (PubPeer FAQ). There are also good reasons why science needs a way to verify published work other than critiques published by journals, because journals make such critiques difficult. Of 330 top-ranked journals across 22 disciplines, only 63% accepted post-publication critique at all, and those that did often limited it (Hardwicke et al., 2022).

23%
of a random sample of psychology journals offered an explicit way to submit a critique of a published article (Whamond et al., 2025).


1,000 words
was the median length limit for critiques of published articles at top-ranked journals (Hardwicke et al., 2022).


12 weeks
was the median time allowed after the original article’s publication to submit a critique (Hardwicke et al., 2022).

Even among the most prominent psychology journals, only 38% did, and almost no articles in either sample had a published critique (Whamond et al., 2025). Concerns about data integrity often take far longer than a few weeks to find, and need more than 400 words to document. Journal limits were found to be as strict as 175 words and two weeks (Hardwicke et al., 2022). These represent severe misalignment between publishing processes and the putative goal of the scientific record, which is to pursue truth. PubPeer is, arguably, a symptom of the very flawed way that critiques of published work are treated by the publishing system.
Others argue that PubPeer comments are mostly about trivial points such as typos, or are unprofessional personal attacks. The large-scale evidence says otherwise. In a classification of 17,244 articles commented on PubPeer, the comments on 82.9% reported manipulation, potential publishing fraud, methodological flaws, or honest but serious errors. The largest single category was manipulation of data or images (Ortega & Delgado-Quirós, 2023; see also Ortega, 2022). PubPeer’s own rules require comments to be based on “publicly verifiable information” and polite, neutral, and factual. They forbid allegations of misconduct and personal comments about authors, and moderators do not publish comments that break them (PubPeer FAQ).
Some authors object to anonymous PubPeer comments, without asking why anonymity is allowed. Researchers who report serious concerns about published work have repeatedly faced legal action. In 2014, the cancer researcher Fazlul Sarkar sued to make PubPeer reveal the identities of anonymous commenters who had pointed out problems with images in his papers. PubPeer, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, won on appeal in 2016 (The Scientist), and Sarkar has since had dozens of papers retracted (Retraction Watch). In 2023, Francesca Gino sued the three researchers behind the Data Colada blog, who had reported evidence of data fabrication in her work, for $25 million for defamation. The claims against them were dismissed in 2024 (Poets & Quants), and Harvard revoked her tenure in 2025. Even unsuccessful lawsuits cost the people who are sued time, money, and stress, and anonymity protects people, especially early-career researchers, who could not otherwise afford to report what they find. In the Gino/Data Colada case, the researchers’ universities initially said they would not support their legal defense as critique of others’ research was not part of their official duties. After public outcry and a GoFundMe campaign raised more than $250k, the universities eventually agreed to cover some of the legal costs - but likely for PR reasons more than any commitment to the idea that the lawsuit was a threat to academic freedom.
PubPeer’s browser extension, available for Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari, checks every article you read for PubPeer comments and shows a banner at the top of the page if it finds any. This turns PubPeer from a site you have to remember to search into one that alerts you as you read. I highly recommend installing it.

title: 17  Reference and citation methods ✎ Draft
text:
17.1 Nonexistent and hallucinated references
An article’s reference list is part of its evidence. Each citation is a claim that another document exists, and that it says what the citing article says it says. Both claims can be checked. This chapter covers three ways they can fail:
The first two problems can now be screened for semi-automatically. The third still mostly requires carefully reading and checking the cited articles.
A nonexistent reference points to an article that does not exist. Some are fabricated outright and bear no relationship to any published article. Others may bear some resemblance to a published article, e.g., sharing a similar name or authorship but with other details incorrect - often the DOI resolves to a totally unrelated article. Many of these come from large language models. Others are real articles cited with the wrong title, authors, year, or DOI, so that the reference cannot be traced to the document it is supposed to point to.
These references are already common in the published literature and becoming more so. Topaz et al. (2026) checked around 2.5 million articles in PubMed Central and found 4,046 fabricated citations in 2,810 of them.
Zhao et al. (2026) found the same trend across arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN, and PubMed Central. The rate of references that could not be matched to any published work rose sharply from mid-2024, and the authors estimated rates of hallucinated citations in 2025 of 0.27% for PubMed Central and 1.91% for SSRN. Neither study can show that any one fabricated reference was produced by a language model; paper mills and deliberate manipulation produce them too. Either way, they passed whatever editorial checks the articles went through.
A single nonexistent reference is not by itself evidence that an article’s results are untrustworthy. It does show that at least part of the text was not checked by its authors, and it raises questions about how the rest of the article was produced. Several nonexistent references, especially ones cited for key claims, are a more serious concern.

title: 17  Reference and citation methods ✎ Draft
text:
1 in 277
biomedical articles published in early 2026 contained a fabricated reference, up from 1 in 2,828 in 2023 (Topaz et al., 2026).









NoteExample: a reference whose DOI leads to an unrelated article



Baldeo (2026) reported that heavy use of generative AI was associated with lower confidence in one’s own reasoning. It was promoted in a press release by the American Psychological Association, the journal’s publisher, titled “Overreliance on AI programs may undermine confidence at work”. It was then covered by Time (“Letting AI do your work erodes your confidence, according to a new study”) and Futurism (“Study finds AI use eats away at users’ confidence in their own brains”).
Its reference list contained only nine references. Commenters on PubPeer - including myself, Sandra Grinchgl, Malte Elson, and Jamie Cummins - found that one of them, attributed to Clemenson, Stark, and Stark (2021) in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, could not be found anywhere. Its DOI led to a different article: Tompary and Thompson-Schill’s (2021) “Semantic influences on episodic memory distortions”. Two other references were real, but were cited for claims about cognitive offloading that they did not make, one of the problems covered in Section 17.2.
The commenters also raised many other concerns, including regression results that were mathematically impossible given the reported correlations (see Chapter 11), implausible recruitment, and measures that did not match the article’s claims. The journal opened an investigation and retracted the article in August 2026 (American Psychological Association, 2026). As Retraction Watch reported, the company that granted ethical approval for the study was a company founded and run by the author, meaning that the study had not actually received independent ethical review. The APA’s press release now carries a retraction notice; the Time and Futurism articles do not.



17.1.1 Automated tools
Checking whether a reference exists is tedious by hand, but simple to automate: extract each reference, search for it in bibliographic databases such as Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and PubMed, and flag references with no close match. Many open-source tools now do this. They differ in three ways that matter to most readers:

Ease of use. Some run in the browser and need no installation (e.g., CheckIfExist, CiteScan, and CiteAudit). Others must be installed locally and run from the command line or a local web interface (e.g., Hallucinator, RefChecker, and HalRef).
Cost. Most are free. Some features depend on paid services; for example, RefChecker’s hallucination check needs access to a language model with web search.
Validation. Few have been tested independently, and several are tuned to the reference formats and databases of computer science, which makes them less suitable for psychology and medicine.

Badalova & Mayr (2026) compared five of these tools on 104 references from three documents, which they had checked by hand: 71 genuine references and 33 problematic ones, such as references with incorrect titles, mismatched authors or journals, unresolvable or incorrect DOIs, or no traceable source.

Table 17.1 shows a trade-off between sensitivity (the proportion of problematic references a tool flags) and specificity (the proportion of genuine references it accepts). A tool can catch more problematic references by being stricter about what counts as a match, but the same strictness makes it flag more genuine references whose details are slightly off. The tools that caught the most problematic references also flagged around half of the genuine references, and the tool with the fewest false alarms missed almost half of the problematic references. No tool did well on both. The main causes of false alarms were errors in extracting references from PDFs, sensitivity to formatting, and gaps in database coverage (e.g., books, reports, and very recent or non-English work). The test set is also small. These tools are therefore screening tools: every flagged reference has to be checked by hand, by searching for its title and DOI, before anything is said about it.
For now, I recommend CheckIfExist (Abbonato, 2026). It caught 31 of the 33 problematic references in Badalova & Mayr (2026)’s comparison, it is free, and it runs as a web app with no login. It accepts a full PDF or Word document, a BibTeX file, or pasted references, and checks them against Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and OpenAlex. These are general-purpose databases, so it is a reasonable fit for psychology and medicine.

CheckIfExist
Free web app, no login required: zabbonat.github.io/References-Validation







Figure 17.1: The CheckIfExist web app. Paste one or more references, or upload a PDF, Word, or BibTeX file, then run a Quick Check (one reference) or Batch Check (several).



CheckIfExist’s sensitivity is good, but its specificity is not: it also flagged 34 of the 71 genuine references. So in Badalova & Mayr (2026)’s comparison, about half of the references it flagged were in fact fine. In a typical article the proportion will be worse, because most reference lists contain few or no problematic references, so most of the flags will be false alarms. A flag from CheckIfExist means only that a reference needs checking, not that it is nonexistent. Check each flagged reference by hand before drawing any conclusions about it.

title: 17  Reference and citation methods ✎ Draft
section: 17.2 Citations of articles that exist but do not support the claim
text:
17.2 Citations of articles that exist but do not support the claim
The most common citation problem cannot be caught by checking that a reference exists. A real, unretracted article can still be cited for something it does not say. In medicine this is often called “quotation accuracy”; Cobb et al. (2023) call it “miscitation”.
To the best of my knowledge, it is currently quite rare for such inaccuracies or miscitations to be the basis of a retraction. It is unclear whether this is due to journals/publishers not viewing this as a serious problem, or whether reports to research integrity offices do not tend to references such issues. Nonetheless, a high prevalence of miscitation of the literature may undermine an article’s trustworthiness.
crumbs: 17  Reference and citation methods [✎ Draft]{.badge .badge-draft2}

title: 17  Reference and citation methods ✎ Draft
text:
17.3 Estimates from psychology
Cobb et al. (2023) checked 3,347 citations of empirical studies in the introductions of 89 articles, from the most recent issues of eight leading psychology journals. Two independent coders compared each citing claim to the methods and results of the cited article. Each citation was coded as accurate, somewhat accurate (correct in broad terms, but omitting an important qualifier, e.g., describing an effect found only in boys as an effect in children), or inaccurate (the claim was never examined in the cited article, or the cited article found the opposite). When coders could not agree, the citation was given the more lenient code.

19%
of 3,347 citations in 89 articles in eight leading psychology journals were only ‘somewhat accuate’, e.g., failed to include important nuance of the article they cited (Cobb et al., 2023).


10%
of citations completely mischaracterized the results of the article cited, e.g., the cited article did not examine the claim or found the opposite (Cobb et al., 2023).

Of the 318 inaccurate citations, 195 cited an article for something it never assessed, and 123 cited an article for a result it contradicted. Rates varied between journals. The Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology had the most miscitations, at 28.7%, which is more than one in four. Miscitation was not related to the number of authors or the seniority of the first author.
These are probably underestimates for the literature as a whole. The journals were among the most prestigious in their fields, and disagreements between coders were resolved in the authors’ favour.

17.3.1 Estimates from medicine
Miscitation has been studied for longer in medicine, where it is usually called a “quotation error”. Jergas & Baethge (2015) meta-analysed 28 studies of quotation accuracy in medical journal articles.

25%
(95% CI [19.5, 32.4]) of citations in medical journal articles contain a quotation error (Jergas & Baethge, 2015).


12%
(95% CI [8.4, 16.6]) of citations contain a major quotation error (Jergas & Baethge, 2015).

Heterogeneity between studies was substantial, but even the lowest estimate was 6.7%. Citations of secondary rather than original sources accounted for less than one sixth of the errors. Mogull (2017) reanalysed 15 such studies, counting errors per citing statement rather than per reference, and estimated a lower overall rate of 14.5% (95% CI [10.5, 18.6]). About two thirds of these errors (64.8%) were major: the cited source did not support the claim, was unrelated to it, or contradicted it.
Individual studies show the same pattern in specific fields:

In 250 randomly selected citations from the five highest-impact orthopaedic and sports medicine journals, 13.6% were not fully supported by the cited article, and 2.8% were completely unsupported (Gazendam et al., 2021).
In 2,995 articles citing 13 highly cited nephrology papers, 15% contained at least one inaccurate citation of those papers. The most common problem was citing a finding the cited article did not report (38.4% of inaccurate citations), and one fifth of the inaccurate citations repeated an earlier inaccurate citation rather than the original article (Pavlovic et al., 2021).
A 2010 commentary criticising the Newcastle-Ottawa scale, a tool widely used to rate the quality of observational studies in systematic reviews, had been cited more than 1,250 times by 2016. In a random sample of 100 articles citing it, 96 were systematic reviews, and 94 of these (98%) cited it as support for using the scale: the opposite of what it argued (Stang et al., 2018).

The last example shows how miscitation spreads. Once a few authors cite an article for the wrong conclusion, later authors copy the citation without reading the original.


17.3.2 Checking citations by hand
No validated automated tool yet checks whether a cited article supports a claim, so this check still means reading. It is not feasible to check every citation in an article, so focus on the citations that matter most:

citations that support the study’s rationale and hypotheses;
citations given as justification for methods, such as measures described as “validated” or analyses described as “standard”;
citations used to interpret the results, especially claims that the results agree with previous research.

For each one, find the cited article and read its methods and results, not just its abstract. Check that the cited study examined the claim, in the population the citing article describes, and found what the citing article says it found. Citations of reviews and meta-analyses need particular care, because they are often cited as evidence for a general effect that the review itself found to vary or to be absent in some studies.
A few miscitations are, unfortunately, normal. They are a concern for trustworthiness when they are concentrated in the claims an article depends on, or when they all point the same way: towards making the article’s own hypotheses look better supported than the cited literature suggests.

title: 17  Reference and citation methods ✎ Draft
text:
17.4 Citations of retracted articles
Checking whether references have been retracted is a separate check from checking whether they exist. A retracted reference does exist, but it has been withdrawn from the record, often because its results could not be trusted. Citations of retracted work matter for two reasons.
First, an article that builds its rationale, methods, or interpretation on retracted work may inherit that work’s problems.
Second, several citations of retracted work are a warning sign that the citing article came from a paper mill.
Paper mills are businesses that sell research articles, and authorship on them, to researchers who need publications, for example to be promoted or to graduate. They produce manuscripts to order, often from templates, with fabricated or recycled data and images. They then get them into journals, in some cases by bribing editors or by arranging entire special issues. They operate at an industrial scale, and their output appears to be growing faster than the legitimate literature. For accessible introductions, see:

The fight against fake-paper factories that churn out sham science (Holly Else and Richard Van Noorden, Nature, 2021);
Paper mills are bribing editors at scholarly journals, Science investigation finds (Frederik Joelving, Science, 2024);
Scientific fraud has become an ‘industry,’ alarming analysis finds (Science, 2025).

Paper mills tend to cite their own earlier products, to pad out reference lists and to raise the mill’s citation counts. Once a mill is discovered, its products are often retracted in large batches. Articles from the same mill then have reference lists full of retracted articles. A reference list with several retracted articles is a flag in its own right, especially when they come from the same journal, special issue, or group of authors. It suggests the article may share their origin, whatever its own results look like.

17.4.1 Feet of Clay
Guillaume Cabanac’s Problematic Paper Screener (Cabanac et al., 2022) includes a “Feet of Clay” detector (Cabanac, 2022), named after the Biblical image of a statue on a fragile base. It flags published articles that cite retracted articles, or articles flagged on PubPeer. It uses the retraction notices registered with Crossref, which now include the Retraction Watch Database. Each flagged article gets a report listing its problematic references, and you can also look up which articles cite a given retracted article. It covers the literature indexed by Dimensions, and its lists are updated periodically rather than in real time.
To check a single article’s references yourself, you can also enter each cited DOI into the post-publication notice checker in Section 16.6. Reference managers such as Zotero also flag retracted items in your library, which helps authors avoid the problem in the first place.


17.4.2 Interpreting citations of retracted articles
Citing a retracted article is not always a problem. The citation may predate the retraction, the article may be cited precisely because it was retracted, or it may be cited for a minor point. What matters is how many retracted articles are cited, what they are cited for, whether they were cited after the retraction notice, and whether they cluster in a way that suggests a common source. An article whose main hypothesis or method depends on a retracted study is a concern. So is one with many retracted references from the same journal or authors. An article that cites a single retracted study in passing, among a dozen others, usually is not.

title: 24  Trustworthiness Assessment and INSPECT-SR ✎ Draft
text:
24.1 Cochrane
Cochrane (formerly the Cochrane Collaboration) is an international network of researchers, health professionals, and patients that produces systematic reviews of the evidence on healthcare interventions. It was founded in 1993 and is named after the epidemiologist Archie Cochrane. Its reviews are published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, part of the Cochrane Library. Cochrane describes its work as “internationally recognized as the benchmark for high-quality information about the effectiveness of health care” (Cochrane, n.d.-a).
A Cochrane Review is a systematic review that follows a published protocol. The review authors search for every study that meets prespecified eligibility criteria, appraise each study, extract its data, and, where appropriate, combine the results in a meta-analysis. Cochrane Reviews aim “to provide the best available evidence of the effects of healthcare interventions”, but the quality of that evidence “depends, inevitably, upon the reliability of the studies included” (Cochrane, n.d.-a).
crumbs: 24  Trustworthiness Assessment and INSPECT-SR [✎ Draft]{.badge .badge-draft2}

title: 24  Trustworthiness Assessment and INSPECT-SR ✎ Draft
text:
24.1.1 Risk of Bias
The established way to appraise the trials in a review is a Risk of Bias assessment. Cochrane’s original tool for randomised controlled trials was published in 2011 (Higgins et al., 2011) and was later replaced by RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019). RoB 2 asks whether the design, conduct, or analysis of a trial could have biased its estimate of the effect, across five domains: the randomisation process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result.
Risk of Bias assessment takes a trial’s report at face value. It asks whether the trial, as described, was likely to produce a biased estimate. It does not ask whether the trial was actually conducted as described, or whether the numbers it reports are possible or real.


24.1.2 Problematic studies
That assumption fails for problematic studies: studies “where there are serious questions about the trustworthiness of the data or findings, regardless of whether the study has been formally retracted” (Cochrane, n.d.-a). A study can be problematic because of misconduct, such as fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism, but also because of poor research practices or honest critical errors.

24.1.2.1 How common are problematic studies?
While good estimates of prevalence do not yet exist, there is reason to believe that problematic trials are not rare.
For example, Carlisle analysed the 526 randomised controlled trials submitted to the journal Anaesthesia between February 2017 and March 2020 (Carlisle, 2021). He judged that 73 (14%) contained false data, and that 43 (8%) were “zombie” trials, which he considered fatally flawed. These rates depended strongly on what he could see. Among the 153 trials whose authors supplied individual patient data, 44% had false data and 26% were zombie trials, compared with 2% and 1% of the 373 trials assessed from summary data alone. This suggests that most problematic trials go undetected when only the published report is available.
Estimates from outside clinical trials point the same way. The most widely cited figure comes from surveys of researchers: about 2% admit to having fabricated or falsified data at least once (Fanelli, 2009, summarised in Heathers, 2024). Heathers argues that this underestimates the problem. People are unlikely to admit to misconduct, even in anonymous surveys, and the share of researchers who have ever faked a result says little about how much of the published literature is fake. He instead collected 12 studies that estimated the proportion of papers with fabricated or falsified elements (Heathers, 2024), including:

A visual inspection of 20,621 papers in 40 biomedical journals, which found inappropriately duplicated images in 3.8% of them, and about 4% of those published from 2005 onwards.
An analysis of 588 preclinical studies of chronic stress models of depression, of which 13.9% contained image anomalies consistent with manipulation.
A GRIM analysis of 71 psychology articles, half of which reported at least one impossible mean (Brown & Heathers, 2017). GRIM is described in Section 12.2. After requesting the authors’ data, Heathers puts the proportion with hallmarks of manipulation between 4.2% and 16.9%.
The editor-in-chief of Molecular Brain, who asked for the raw data behind 41 of the 180 manuscripts he handled between 2017 and 2019, because their results looked “too beautiful to be true” (Miyakawa, 2020). Twenty-one were withdrawn without providing raw data, and 19 of the remaining 20 were rejected because the raw data were insufficient. In seven of these, the raw data did not match the reported results. Only one manuscript was sent for peer review. Miyakawa notes that he cannot know how many of these manuscripts contained fabricated data. Heathers’ estimate of 14.4% of all submissions rests on a hypothetical figure in the editorial: if an informal poll of researchers were right, 26 of the 40 withdrawn or rejected manuscripts would contain fabricated data.
A COPE and STM report on paper mills, which found that, on average, 14% of the manuscripts submitted to the journals it examined between 2019 and 2021 were suspect, ranging from 2% to 46% by journal.

Across the 16 estimates in these studies, the median was 14%, and 9 of the 16 fell between 13.4% and 16.9%. Heathers concludes that roughly 1 in 7 papers contain errors consistent with faking in at least one element. It’s quite important to emphasise that many commentators have problems with this estimate, including myself. If I was to reframe Heathers’ argument, I would do it as so: Collectively, we are acting as if the prevalence of untrustworthy articles is so small that it can literally be ignored. There is sufficient reason to act as if the prevalence of untrustworthy research is much higher than this, and we should at least look for it.
More recent studies report similar or higher rates in specific fields. Aquarius and colleagues assessed every article that was eligible for a systematic review of preclinical studies of microvascular injury after myocardial infarction, using the image-analysis software Imagetwin together with visual checks (Aquarius et al., 2026). They had decided in advance to exclude problematic articles from the review. Of 201 articles, 57 (28.4%) were deemed problematic: 46 because of duplicated or manipulated images, and 11 because of inappropriately duplicated values in tables. Only three of the 57 had previously been flagged on PubPeer for serious concerns. Similar assessments within other systematic reviews of animal studies found image-related problems in 19% of included articles on depression and 40% of included articles on early brain injury after subarachnoid haemorrhage (both summarised in Aquarius et al., 2026). These studies are examples of trustworthiness assessment as part of a systematic review: every eligible study was checked, and problematic studies were excluded before synthesis.


24.1.2.2 Problematic studies change the conclusions of reviews
A review of 847 systematic reviews that included at least one retracted trial found that excluding the retracted trials changed the size of the pooled effect in 16% of meta-analyses, and its direction in just over 8% (summarised in Wilkinson et al., 2026). Retraction can take years, if it happens at all, so retraction status alone cannot identify problematic trials. Risk of Bias tools are not designed to detect these problems, and do not appear to succeed in doing so (Wilkinson et al., 2026).


24.1.2.3 Cochrane’s policy on problematic studies
Cochrane’s policy for managing potentially problematic studies sets out what review authors and editors should do (Cochrane, n.d.-a, n.d.-b):

Retracted studies must not be included in a Cochrane Review. They are listed as excluded, with a citation to the retraction notice.
Studies with an Expression of Concern should be treated “with a high degree of caution”. Whether they are excluded depends on the reason for the concern, because some Expressions of Concern relate to matters that do not affect the validity of the data, such as authorship disputes.
Studies with no post-publication notice, but where the review team has concerns, should be checked against bibliographic databases, the Retraction Watch Database, PubPeer, and the publisher’s website. The review team should contact the study authors for clarification, and if concerns remain, write to the journal editor in neutral language. Meanwhile, the study is classified as “Awaiting Classification” rather than included.

The implementation guidance notes that “there is no standard definition of, nor validated method to identify, a problematic study”, and that it will be updated as evidence and consensus emerge (Cochrane, n.d.-b). INSPECT-SR was developed to provide such a method. In October 2025, Cochrane endorsed it as an optional tool for review authors who wish to assess the trustworthiness of the randomised controlled trials in their reviews (Cochrane, 2025).



24.1.3 Trustworthiness Assessment vs. science sleuthing
Trustworthiness Assessment and science sleuthing use many of the same methods, and the people who develop them often overlap. They differ in how studies are chosen, how the checks are carried out, and what the result is used for.









Trustworthiness Assessment
Science sleuthing




Which studies
Every trial that is eligible for a systematic review, whether or not anything seems wrong with it
Articles are selected via heterogeneous means


Process
Structured: the same checks for every study, a recorded response to each check, judgments per domain and overall, and ideally two independent reviewers who then reach consensus
Open-ended: follows whatever leads seem most promising for that study


Complexity
Checks are often shallower to facilitate speed and lower training burden
Checks are often deeper as they are (currently) performed by more expert sleuths, with more attention paid to fewer articles. Exceptions to this exist, e.g., image forensics work conducted by Elisabeth Bik, Rene Aquarius, Matthew Shrank and others often involve thousands of articles


Purpose
To decide whether a study’s data can be used in a particular evidence synthesis
To correct the scientific record, for example by alerting journals and institutions or posting on PubPeer


Outcome
Studies with serious concerns are excluded from the review, and studies with some concerns are examined in sensitivity analyses
Corrections, Expressions of Concern, retractions, and sometimes misconduct investigations


Stance on misconduct
Explicitly not a test for fraud: concerns about trustworthiness “do not constitute an accusation of research misconduct” (Wilkinson et al., 2026)
May raise the question of misconduct, although findings are usually framed as concerns to be resolved by journals and institutions



How studies are selected also changes what a positive result means. A check that flags a trial chosen because it already looked suspicious is more likely to point to a problem than the same flag in a trial selected only because it met a review’s eligibility criteria. Trustworthiness Assessment is applied to many trials that have no problems at all, so false positives matter more there, and judgments should rest on the guidance for each check rather than on a single flag.

title: 24  Trustworthiness Assessment and INSPECT-SR ✎ Draft
text:
24.2 INSPECT-SR domains and checks
INSPECT-SR (Investigating Problematic Clinical Trials in Systematic Reviews) is a tool for assessing the trustworthiness of randomised controlled trials (Wilkinson et al., 2026). It was developed in five stages:

A list of 76 candidate checks was drawn from the existing literature and a survey of experts.
The checks were applied to the trials in 50 Cochrane Reviews to assess how feasible they were and how much difference they made.
A two-round Delphi survey (148 and 134 participants) found expert consensus for 29 checks.
Eight online consensus meetings narrowed these to 21 checks and decided how each should be applied.
User testing and a workshop refined the wording and the guidance. Testers took a median of 45 minutes to assess a trial.

The final tool has 21 checks in four domains, shown in the table below. Each check is answered “yes”, “no”, “unclear”, or “not applicable”, where “yes” indicates a potential problem. After each domain, the reviewer judges whether there are no concerns, some concerns, or serious concerns about the trial in that domain. The overall judgment for the study should usually be at least as severe as the most severe domain judgment. There is no algorithm that converts answers into judgments: a single “yes” does not automatically mean serious concerns, although some, such as a retraction (check 1.1), usually will.
The article recommends that INSPECT-SR is applied to every eligible trial in a systematic review, before Risk of Bias assessment and data extraction, by two reviewers working independently. Trials with serious concerns should be excluded, and trials with some concerns should be examined in sensitivity analyses. Checks 1.1 and 1.2 should be repeated shortly before the review is completed, because new notices may have been published in the meantime. INSPECT-SR can be used for trials in any area of healthcare and does not require individual participant data. It does not assess Risk of Bias, generalisability, or conflicts of interest. Extensions are in development or planned for individual participant data (INSPECT-IPD), non-randomised studies (INSPECT-NRS), and use by journal editors (INSPECT-JR).
The wording of each check is short, and users should not try to infer how to apply a check from its wording alone (Wilkinson et al., 2026). The INSPECT-SR Guidance website explains each check with examples, provides an editable template for recording assessments, and is updated as the tool is used and evaluated.
I am one of the co-authors of the INSPECT-SR article and contributed to its guidance document. With Jack Wilkinson, I maintain the INSPECT-SR Guidance website, whose source code is on GitHub. Lukas Jung and I also developed an app for check 4.8, which the article recommends to users. This book is not part of the official INSPECT-SR guidance. It aims to explain the methods behind many of the checks in more depth, and the table below shows which chapters are relevant to each check.

title: 26  Forensic meta-science methods require validation ✎ Outline
text:
26.1 Proposed standard
Many forensic meta-science methods have been developed by non methodologists. This is probably not accidental: maybe it required some outside thinkers to develop the agonizingly simple math that GRIM is based on.
But, now that these methods have been conceived of, they need to be validated. There is an asymmetric reputational risk here: if we use these methods to determine that other research is untrustworthy, and it is in fact our methods that are untrustworthy, we are going to look quite silly. This is where the (quantitative) forensic meta-science research community is currently falling behind, and which work in our research group tries to improve.
At the same time, traditional methods validation in the sense of a simulation study under ideal conditions is insufficient here. Trustworthiness assessments are increasingly likely to be conducted by users of forensic meta-science methods rather than expert developers of these methods. As such, implementations of the methods need to be usable, they need to have UIs that guide users towards making sensible choices and away from non-sensible ones, and they need to have clearly specified interpretations of results and reporting guidelines, etc. We therefore conceptualise validation to be broader, along the following candidate dimensions.
This rubric defines actionable roadmaps for specification, validation, improvement, and the assessment of readiness (rather than being merely aspirational).
Properties
Usage
Ecosystem

title: 26  Forensic meta-science methods require validation ✎ Outline
text:
Formal specification of method


Logic, math, etc.
Scope of inference
Assumptions
Limitations
Use and failure cases


Implementation


In a free and open-source software library written in an open-source programming language, such as R or Python. In R library or equivalent.
Code as primary output. Treat the implementation as the artefact under review. Open code, unit tests, reproducible fixtures, ;continuous integration.
This often involves additional considerations beyond the abstract method to handle real world use cases. Common considerations include data extraction, which is a whole realm of tasks in itself.
Note that separation of library and tool is important for validation.


Validation against simulated data


e.g., Monte Carlo for stochastic methods, parameter sweep for deterministic methods, etc., to assess whether the method functions as expected over a wide range of known inputs. ADEMP reporting.
Using common performance metrics from research methods, such as sensitivity, specificity, empirical rejection rate (calibration under the null, ability and power to detect issues of what size), bias, coverage, etc.
Robustness to nuisance parameters (e.g., rounded inputs and different rounding or truncation conventions, reporting standards, typos in inputs, number of items).


Validation against human-coded data


To assess whether the method functions as expected over a wide range of realistic inputs. This is useful for surfacing issues to do with extraction/parsing, edge cases, etc.
Consideration of gold vs. reference standards, reporting of inter-rater reliability between human-human, human-tool, or human-ai coders, etc.
This provides information on generalisability, validation within specific domains (e.g., reporting standards may differ between psychology and medicine; pdf formatting may differ between journals or publishers).


Large scale application


Substantive conclusions (e.g., re prevalence, severity etc) from applying the method to a large amount of real world data. Often (initially) using the same data used for validation against human coding, as part of the same process.


Adversarial robustness / gameability.


Once a method is known, can it be evaded (e.g., reporting choices that defeat GRIM)? What vectors of gamability might exist?



Tool


Implementation of the library in a UI tool (eg Shiny app), AI skill, etc. to increase usability/scalability.
Audit trail: does the tool produce an auditable trail of inputs, outputs, versions of method/tool applied, etc.


Reporting standards


Instructions on how to interpret and report results from the method/tool.


Training materials


Materials that train and ideally assess whether users can correctly use and report the method/tool, including its assumptions, limitations, use- and failure-cases etc.


Usability


Evidence that users find the library/tool to be adequately usable; and that misuse cases are assessed, detected and mitigated via human factors research.



Comparison


When multiple implementations of a given or related method are available, head-to-head comparisons are informative. This can be along many of the above dimensions, from validation to usability to training materials, to a general assessment of use-cases.
Versioning, maintenance & deprecation.
Versioning of methods/tools.
Last time of validation. Tools rot (PDF formats change, R deps break). Need for ongoing validation, not one-shot.


Readiness


TBD: Some sort of maturity-level or evidence-readiness scheme that integrates the above.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
27.1 Three layers
A forensic check is usually referred to by a single name: “statcheck flagged this result”, or “this mean fails GRIM”. But every result from a check involves three different things: a method, an implementation of that method, and a tool through which the implementation is used. Each of them can fail, and they fail in different ways. When a check gives an unexpected answer, the first question to ask is which of the three produced it. Treating them as one thing leads to blaming the maths for an error in reading a PDF, or trusting the output of a web page as if it were the maths.
statcheck (Section 11.1.1) is a good example, because “statcheck” can refer to at least three different things, and each can fail in its own way:
The same three layers are present in every check in this book. GRIM is a method, the grim() function in {scrutiny} is an implementation of it, and a web app that calls that function is a tool. The calculators in Chapter 11 are tools that use the implementations in the {recalc} R package.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
What it is
How it can fail




The method
The maths: recalculating a p-value from a test statistic and its degrees of freedom, and the interval that accounts for rounding.
It cannot fail, in the sense that it is provably correct given its inputs and assumptions. But the assumptions may not hold: the test may be one-sided, the p-value may have been corrected, or the degrees of freedom may have been rounded. This can come from the user choosing the wrong settings, or from the article not reporting what was done.


The implementation
The {statcheck} R package: code that applies the method, with particular defaults and decision rules.
Code can contain errors that only arise under particular conditions. Defaults and rules differ between versions, such as whether one-sided tests are searched for, whether p = .000 counts as an error, and whether p = .05 counts as significant. Results from different versions are not always comparable.


The tool
A way of accessing the implementation more easily, such as the web app at statcheck.io, which extracts text from an uploaded file and passes it to the R package.
It may fail to extract the results from the file, or extract them incorrectly. Parsing PDFs is notoriously hard. Different tools that use the same R package can return different results for the same article, because they extract the text differently, such as statcheck.io and statcheck.steveharoz.com.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
27.2 What failed?
Keeping the three layers apart makes it clearer what a result means and what to do next. A disagreement between two tools about the same article is usually a disagreement about extraction, not about the maths. A flag that disappears once the right assumption is applied (e.g., one-sided) is a question about the article’s reporting, not about the implementation. And a flag that survives every reasonable assumption, after the numbers have been checked against the original text by hand, is a genuine inconsistency in the method’s own terms.
Each of the problems with statcheck described in Section 11.1.1.4 belongs to one of the layers, and the layer determines what should be done about it:








What happened
Layer
What to do




statcheck.io and statcheck.steveharoz.com give different results for the same article
Tool: the text was extracted differently
Check the extracted text against the article


A χ² statistic is read as a statistic named “2” (Schmidt, 2017)
Tool: the PDF was misread
Check the extracted text against the article


p = .000 is counted as an error
Implementation: a default decision rule (pZeroError = TRUE)
Decide whether a reporting convention counts as an error, and set the option accordingly


The same text gets different results from two versions of the package
Implementation: the versions have different options and defaults, such as robust_rounding (Section 11.1.1.1)
Report the version used, and use the same version for results that will be compared


A result is flagged, but is consistent as a one-sided test
Method: an assumption does not hold
Read the article for whether the test was one-sided


A Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-value is flagged
Method: an assumption does not hold
Read the article for corrections to the p-value



Only the last two say anything about the article, and even they do not say that it contains an error. They say that the article does not report enough to know which assumption is right.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
27.3 Separation within each layer
Each layer can be divided further, and the same reasoning applies within it: when something fails, it helps to know which part failed.
Within the method, the mathematical identity is distinct from the assumptions needed to apply it and from the decision rules built on top of it. That a two-sided p-value follows from t and its degrees of freedom is an identity. That the test was two-sided, and that the p-value was not corrected afterwards, are assumptions. That a reported p-value is an “inconsistency” if it lies outside the recalculated interval, and a “gross” one if the two fall on opposite sides of α = .05, are decision rules. The identity cannot be wrong, but the assumptions can be, and the decision rules are choices that others might make differently.
Within the implementation, the code that computes the result is distinct from its defaults, from how it handles unusual inputs, and from what it does with inputs that it does not use. Each of these can fail even when the computation is correct. Some examples from the development of {recalc}, the package behind the calculators in Chapter 11:

A default that changed the answer. The subgroup functions require the number of decimal places of every input, and sample sizes were usually given as 0 decimal places. This treats a count as if it had been rounded to the nearest whole number, which lets a reported N that differs from the sum of the subgroups’ ns by a participant or two pass as consistent. Counts are exact, and are now treated as such (Section 11.3.1.1). The maths was right; the default was not.
An edge case that broke the code. The profile likelihood confidence interval for an odds ratio was calculated by fitting a logistic regression and profiling it. When one of the four counts is zero, the model cannot be fitted properly, and the code returned a lower limit of 0 instead of the correct value of about 2. The method, inverting the likelihood ratio test, was fine. Its implementation failed on an input it was not designed for, without any warning.
An input that was accepted but ignored. A function accepted a reported confidence interval for Cohen’s d, but never compared it with the recalculated one. The output therefore never flagged an inconsistent interval, and a reader could easily take the absence of a flag for a pass.

None of these is visible from the maths. They are only found by testing the implementation against the method directly, for example by checking its output against a slow but transparent calculation, or against other implementations, across a wide range of inputs, including unusual ones.
Within the tool, getting the numbers in is distinct from what the tool asks for and infers, and from how it presents the results. Extraction from a PDF is one source of error. What the tool infers is another: the calculators in Chapter 11 take the number of decimal places of each value from the value as it was typed, so a reader who types 4.7 for a reported 4.70 gets a check that allows for more rounding than the article’s numbers had. Presentation is a third: a calculator that says a reported value is “consistent” across a multiverse of analytic choices means that at least one combination of choices could have produced it, not that the authors used that combination.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
27.4 Separation in code
The separation between the layers is worth keeping in code as well as in concepts. The method should be implemented once, in a package function with its own tests, and every tool should call that function rather than reimplementing the maths. Then a fix to the implementation reaches every tool, and the tools cannot quietly disagree with one another about anything except how they get their inputs and display their outputs.
The calculators in this book are built this way. The {recalc} Shiny apps and the webR calculators in Chapter 11 do not reimplement any of the checks. Apart from adding up sample sizes, which needs no R, they call functions in the {recalc} package, and the webR calculators load the package’s code at a fixed version, which they report under their results. The statcheck app in Section 11.1.1.1 does the same with {statcheck}. A tool that copied the formulas into its own code would be a second implementation, and would need testing in its own right.

title: 27  Method, implementation, and tool ✎ Draft
text:
27.5 Reporting
In a trustworthiness assessment, report all three layers, so that a reader can tell which of them a result depends on: the method and the assumptions made in applying it, the implementation and its version and settings, and the tool, including how the numbers were entered or extracted. And check every flagged result by hand against the original text before drawing conclusions from it. A check that fails at the tool or implementation layer says nothing about the article.

title: 28  Validating meta-science methods using simulated data ✎ Outline
text:
This chapter will explain, with worked examples and R/tidyverse/purrr code, how to validate implementations of methods against simulated data. It differentiates between exhaustive grid sweeps and probabilistic Monte Carlo simulations.
This form of validation is essential to understanding whether a method works as expected under idea conditions (i.e., assuming no text extraction, parsing, etc issues; just perfect inputs), in terms of false positives, false negatives, coverage, bias, etc.
